subject: Java
description: Comprehensive, interview-focused Java OOP preparation with core concepts, conceptual questions, tricky Java rules, real-world scenarios and coding examples.

concepts.name: Class
concepts.definition: A blueprint that defines the fields and methods objects of that type can have.
concepts.realWorldExample: A Car class can define colour, model, and start().
javaNotes: A class is a blueprint; declaring a class does not by itself create an instance of that class.
A class can contain fields, methods, constructors, initializer blocks and nested types.
An object is created at runtime using new for ordinary class instances; the reference variable stores a reference, not the object itself.
If no constructor is declared, the compiler supplies a default no-argument constructor. Declaring any constructor prevents that automatic default constructor.
Instance fields receive default values, but local variables must be initialized before they are read.
Use access modifiers to control visibility: private, package-private, protected and public.
Java classes support single inheritance with extends, but can implement multiple interfaces.
An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly; a final class cannot be subclassed.

whyItExists.explanation: A class gives related data and behaviour one named structure. It lets a program describe a kind of thing once and create many objects from the same design.
whyItExists.designProblemSolved: Without a class, a program tends to keep related variables and functions separately. The same structure and rules get repeated for every employee, product, or account, making changes error-prone.
problemsWithoutConcept: Related state and behaviour become scattered across the program.
The same fields and operations are repeatedly declared for similar entities.
There is no clear type boundary describing what data and behaviour belong together.

basicExample.output: No output. A class declaration defines a type; introduce() runs only when it is called on an object.
basicExample.beginnerNote: A class is the definition; an object is the actual instance created from that definition.

walkthrough.approach: Define a class blueprint that groups student state (`name`, `age`) and behavior (`introduce()`) into a single named type without instantiating an object yet.

steps.title: Declare the type boundary
steps.detail: class Student opens a blueprint that tells the compiler what fields and methods every Student instance will possess.

steps.title: Define instance fields
steps.detail: String name and int age declare per-object state; memory for them is allocated only when new Student() is called.

steps.title: Attach behavior to state
steps.detail: introduce() reads name and age directly from the instance on which the method is invoked.

walkthrough.flow: The compiler validates the Student type declaration. Because there is no main method or new Student() call, no heap object is allocated and nothing is printed.
pitfalls: Assuming that declaring a class allocates memory for its instance fields—a class declaration is only metadata until instantiated with new.

keyLines.note: Establishes the Student type blueprint; no instance exists yet.
Instance method that operates on whichever Student object invokes it.

concepts.howItWorksDetailed: When the compiler reads the class declaration, it makes the Student type available for type checking and object creation. The declaration itself does not create a Student instance. Each instance later gets its own instance fields, while the class describes the common set of fields and methods.
concepts.interviewTip: Define a class as a compile-time blueprint that establishes a type boundary; emphasize that memory for instance fields is allocated only when `new` creates an object.

concepts.name: Object
concepts.definition: A runtime instance of a class, with identity, state, and behaviour.
concepts.realWorldExample: car1 and car2 can be separate Car objects with different colours.
javaNotes: An object is a runtime instance of a class and has identity, state and behaviour.
new normally allocates an object and invokes a constructor; the resulting reference can be stored in a variable.
Multiple references can point to the same object, so a mutation through one reference is visible through the others.
Assigning one reference variable to another does not clone the object.
Objects are allocated on the heap in the usual Java object model, while references may be held in local variables or fields.
When an object is no longer reachable from GC roots, it becomes eligible for garbage collection; collection timing is not guaranteed.
== compares object references for identity; equals() compares logical equality only when the class implements that meaning.
An object can be accessed through a superclass or interface reference, enabling runtime polymorphism.

whyItExists.explanation: A class describes a type, but an application usually needs multiple individual entities of that type, each with its own state. Objects provide those individual runtime instances.
whyItExists.designProblemSolved: Without objects, a class would be only a definition and the application would have no separate student, account, or product instances whose state can change independently.
problemsWithoutConcept: There is no individual runtime entity to hold instance state.
Two students cannot naturally have different names and ages using the same class definition.
Behaviour cannot be invoked against a particular instance.

basicExample.beginnerNote: The variables first and second hold references to two distinct objects. The objects have separate instance fields.

walkthrough.approach: Instantiate two distinct Student objects on the heap from the same class blueprint and verify that mutating one object's state does not affect the other.

steps.title: Allocate the first instance
steps.detail: new Student() allocates a Student object on the heap and assigns its reference to first.

steps.title: Allocate a second independent instance
steps.detail: A second new Student() call creates a separate heap object referenced by second, with its own name field.

steps.title: Invoke behavior per instance
steps.detail: Calling first.introduce() and second.introduce() binds this to each respective object and prints its own state.

walkthrough.flow: Main creates two separate Student instances on the heap, assigns first.name = 'Asha' and second.name = 'Ravi', and calls introduce() on each, printing 'Hello, Asha' followed by 'Hello, Ravi'.
pitfalls: Writing Student second = first; thinking it copies the object—that only copies the reference, making both variables point to the same Student instance.

keyLines.note: Allocates the first independent Student instance on the heap.
Allocates a second, completely separate Student instance.

concepts.howItWorksDetailed: For a normal class, new requests object creation and invokes a constructor. The reference variable receives a reference to the object. Instance fields belong to each object, so changing one object’s field does not automatically change another object’s field.
concepts.interviewTip: Distinguish the reference variable (which holds an address/handle) from the heap object itself, and mention that `==` checks reference identity while `equals()` checks logical equality.

concepts.name: Encapsulation
concepts.definition: Bundling data and the methods that operate on it while controlling access to internal state.
concepts.realWorldExample: A BankAccount keeps balance private and validates deposit and withdrawal operations.
javaNotes: Encapsulation bundles data and the methods that operate on that data inside a class.
Fields are commonly declared private so callers cannot modify internal state directly.
Expose controlled operations through methods rather than automatically generating setters for every field.
Validation inside methods or constructors helps keep an object in a valid state.
Getters and setters are not encapsulation by themselves if they expose unrestricted access to every field.
An immutable class typically uses private final fields, controlled construction and no mutators; defensive copies may be needed for mutable field values.
Encapsulation reduces coupling because internal implementation can change without changing callers that use the public contract.
Java access modifiers support encapsulation, but package design and module boundaries also affect visibility.

whyItExists.explanation: Encapsulation protects an object’s internal state and makes the object responsible for enforcing rules whenever that state changes.
whyItExists.designProblemSolved: If callers can change fields directly, they can put an object into an invalid state. A bank balance, for example, could be set to a negative value without a withdrawal rule being checked.
problemsWithoutConcept: Any caller can assign invalid values directly.
Validation rules are duplicated across callers and may be forgotten.
Internal representation becomes tightly coupled to every class using it.

basicExample.beginnerNote: Encapsulation is not simply generating getters and setters. The important part is protecting state and exposing meaningful, controlled operations.

walkthrough.approach: Hide the raw account balance inside a `private` field and force all updates through a validating `deposit(double)` method.

steps.title: Lock down internal state
steps.detail: private double balance = 1000 prevents external callers from setting arbitrary or negative balances directly.

steps.title: Guard mutations inside a domain method
steps.detail: deposit(double amount) checks amount > 0 before adding to balance, silently ignoring or rejecting invalid inputs.

steps.title: Expose read-only state safely
steps.detail: getBalance() returns the current primitive double value without allowing callers to mutate the field.

walkthrough.flow: account starts with balance = 1000.0. account.deposit(500) passes the amount > 0 check and updates balance to 1500.0. account.deposit(-200) fails the check and leaves balance unchanged at 1500.0.
pitfalls: Adding an unvalidated setBalance(double) setter alongside private double balance, which defeats encapsulation by letting callers write negative values.

keyLines.note: Prevents direct field manipulation from outside BankAccount.
Enforces the domain invariant before mutating internal state.

concepts.howItWorksDetailed: Access modifiers define which code can access members. A private field can be read or changed only by code allowed inside its declaring class (including permitted nested access). Public methods form the controlled API. Validation and invariants should live close to the state they protect.
concepts.interviewTip: Stress that encapsulation is about enforcing invariants through intention-revealing domain methods (`deposit`, `withdraw`), not blindly generating public getters and setters for private fields.

concepts.name: Abstraction
concepts.definition: Exposing essential operations while hiding implementation details.
concepts.realWorldExample: A PaymentGateway exposes pay() while hiding whether payment uses UPI or a card.
javaNotes: Objects of an abstract class cannot be created directly using the new keyword.
An abstract class can contain both abstract methods and concrete methods.
An abstract class can have constructors, instance variables, static methods and initialization blocks.
A concrete subclass must implement all inherited abstract methods; otherwise, it must also be declared abstract.
An abstract class does not need to contain an abstract method; it may be abstract simply to prevent direct instantiation.
An abstract method has no method body and must be declared in an abstract class or interface.
Abstract methods cannot be private, static or final because they are intended to be implemented or overridden by a subtype.
Abstraction exposes what a caller can do while hiding how the operation is performed; interfaces and abstract classes are common Java tools for this.

whyItExists.explanation: Abstraction lets callers work with essential operations without needing to understand every implementation detail. It separates what a component promises to do from how it does it.
whyItExists.designProblemSolved: Without abstraction, callers often need to know low-level steps and concrete implementation classes. Replacing an implementation then forces changes in many callers.
problemsWithoutConcept: Client code becomes dependent on implementation details.
Changing an implementation can require changing every caller.
Complex internal steps leak into code that only needs a simple operation.

basicExample.beginnerNote: Abstraction is about exposing a useful contract and hiding unnecessary details. Encapsulation protects internal state; the two ideas are related but not identical.

walkthrough.approach: Separate what an operation does from how it is implemented by programming the caller against a `PaymentService` interface contract.

steps.title: Declare the minimal contract
steps.detail: PaymentService defines pay(double amount) without exposing UPI handles, tokens, or network steps.

steps.title: Implement provider-specific details
steps.detail: UpiPayment implements PaymentService and supplies the concrete UPI payment logic inside pay(double).

steps.title: Bind caller to the abstraction
steps.detail: Main holds a PaymentService reference and calls payment.pay(500), staying decoupled from UpiPayment internals.

walkthrough.flow: Main assigns new UpiPayment() to a PaymentService reference. Calling payment.pay(500) passes compile-time checking against PaymentService and dispatches at runtime to UpiPayment.pay(500), printing 'Paid 500.0 using UPI'.
pitfalls: Leaking provider-specific methods (like verifyUpiPin()) onto the shared PaymentService interface, which forces non-UPI providers to implement irrelevant methods.

keyLines.note: Defines the public contract without implementation details.
Caller depends on the PaymentService abstraction, not the concrete class.

concepts.howItWorksDetailed: Java supports abstraction through interfaces and abstract classes. An interface can declare a contract that implementing classes fulfil. An abstract class can combine abstract operations with shared state or implemented methods. Code typed against the abstraction can work with different implementations.
concepts.interviewTip: Frame abstraction around caller stability: callers depend on what an interface or abstract class promises (`pay()`), staying insulated from provider-specific implementation changes.

concepts.name: Inheritance
concepts.definition: A mechanism through which a subclass derives accessible state and behaviour from a superclass.
concepts.realWorldExample: SavingsAccount extends Account when it is genuinely a specialised kind of account.
javaNotes: Inheritance uses extends to create an is-a relationship between a subclass and a superclass.
Java supports single inheritance of classes: a class can extend only one direct superclass.
A subclass inherits accessible members, but constructors are not inherited.
Private superclass members are not directly accessible by the subclass, although inherited behaviour can use them.
Every class ultimately derives from java.lang.Object, except Object itself.
Use super to access superclass members or invoke a superclass constructor.
Constructors execute from the superclass portion toward the subclass portion; a superclass constructor call must be the first constructor statement when written explicitly.
Java does not support multiple inheritance of classes, but a class can implement multiple interfaces.
Prefer composition over inheritance when the relationship is not genuinely is-a or when inheritance creates tight coupling.
A final class cannot be extended, and a final method cannot be overridden.

whyItExists.explanation: Inheritance models an is-a relationship and allows a specialised class to reuse and extend accessible behaviour from a general class.
whyItExists.designProblemSolved: Without inheritance, genuinely shared behaviour may be copied into several related classes. Fixing a common rule then requires editing each copy and risks inconsistent behaviour.
problemsWithoutConcept: Common behaviour may be duplicated across related types.
A shared change must be repeated in several classes.
There is no subtype relationship for APIs that should accept a general parent type.

basicExample.output:
Animal is eating
Dog is barking
basicExample.beginnerNote: Use inheritance only when the subtype genuinely satisfies the parent type’s contract. Reuse alone is not always a good reason to extend a class.

walkthrough.approach: Model an `IS-A` relationship where `Dog` extends `Animal`, inheriting shared `eat()` behavior while adding specialized `bark()` behavior.

steps.title: Define common base behavior
steps.detail: Animal declares eat(), representing behavior shared by all animal subtypes.

steps.title: Extend the base class
steps.detail: Dog extends Animal inherits accessible members from Animal without duplicating eat().

steps.title: Invoke inherited and specialized methods
steps.detail: A Dog instance can call both the inherited eat() method and its own bark() method.

walkthrough.flow: Main instantiates Dog. Calling dog.eat() resolves to the inherited Animal.eat() method and prints 'Animal is eating'; calling dog.bark() runs Dog.bark() and prints 'Dog is barking'.
pitfalls: Using extends between classes that do not share a true IS-A relationship just to reuse a few lines of code—use composition instead.

keyLines.note: Establishes that Dog IS-A Animal and inherits accessible Animal members.
Invokes the method inherited from Animal on the Dog instance.

concepts.howItWorksDetailed: The extends keyword establishes a superclass/subclass relationship. A subclass inherits accessible members, but constructors are not inherited. A subclass constructor invokes a superclass constructor using super(...) (explicitly or implicitly). Java classes have single class inheritance, though a class can implement multiple interfaces.
concepts.interviewTip: State that inheritance models a strict `IS-A` substitutable relationship (`Liskov Substitution Principle`); if you only want code reuse without substitutability, prefer composition (`HAS-A`).

concepts.name: Polymorphism
concepts.definition: The ability to use a common type for objects with different implementations.
concepts.realWorldExample: A Payment reference can point to UpiPayment or CardPayment.
javaNotes: Polymorphism allows a superclass or interface reference to refer to objects of different implementing or subclass types.
Runtime polymorphism in Java is achieved through method overriding and dynamic method dispatch.
The overridden instance method that runs is selected using the actual object type at runtime, not merely the reference type.
At compile time, the reference type determines which members are accessible and which overloaded method signature is selected.
Overloading is compile-time polymorphism; it is resolved using declared argument types and overload resolution rules.
Static methods are hidden, not overridden; fields are also resolved using the reference type.
Private methods are not overridden because they are not inherited as accessible methods.
An overriding method cannot reduce visibility and cannot declare broader checked exceptions than the overridden method.
Use the @Override annotation so the compiler can detect accidental signature mismatches.
Covariant return types are allowed: an overriding method may return a subtype of the original return type.

whyItExists.explanation: Polymorphism allows code to use one common parent or interface type while the actual object supplies its own behaviour.
whyItExists.designProblemSolved: Without polymorphism, callers often write long if/else or switch statements for every concrete type. Adding a new type then requires changing all those decision points.
problemsWithoutConcept: Callers become coupled to every concrete implementation.
Conditional logic grows whenever a new implementation is added.
Common operations cannot be invoked uniformly through a shared type.

basicExample.beginnerNote: This is runtime polymorphism through method overriding. Method overloading is compile-time polymorphism and is resolved using the method signature and compile-time types.

walkthrough.approach: Hold different subtype instances (`Dog`, `Cat`) in references of their common superclass (`Animal`) and rely on dynamic method dispatch to run each subtype's overridden `sound()` method.

steps.title: Define the overridable base method
steps.detail: Animal declares sound() so any caller with an Animal reference can invoke it.

steps.title: Override behavior in each subtype
steps.detail: Dog and Cat each override sound() with @Override to provide their own implementation.

steps.title: Dispatch at runtime via the base reference
steps.detail: Calling first.sound() and second.sound() on Animal references selects Dog.sound() and Cat.sound() based on the actual heap objects.

walkthrough.flow: first points to a Dog instance and second points to a Cat instance, both typed as Animal. At runtime, first.sound() dispatches to Dog.sound() ('Dog barks') and second.sound() dispatches to Cat.sound() ('Cat meows').
pitfalls: Expecting fields or static methods to behave polymorphically—only overridden instance methods are dynamically dispatched at runtime.

keyLines.note: Upcasts Dog to Animal; compile-time type is Animal, runtime type is Dog.
JVM inspects the runtime object (Dog) to select Dog.sound().

concepts.howItWorksDetailed: For overridden instance methods, Java uses dynamic method dispatch: the runtime class of the object determines which overridden implementation executes. The reference type still controls which members are accessible at compile time. Static methods are hidden rather than overridden, and fields are not dynamically dispatched.
concepts.interviewTip: Contrast compile-time polymorphism (overload resolution based on declared reference/argument types) with runtime polymorphism (dynamic method dispatch based on the actual heap object).

concepts.name: Association, Aggregation and Composition
concepts.definition: Object relationship patterns: association is a general link, aggregation is a weaker whole-part relationship, and composition expresses stronger ownership.
concepts.realWorldExample: A doctor treats patients (association); a department has professors (aggregation); an order owns its line items (composition).
javaNotes: Association is a general relationship in which objects know about or use one another; it does not imply ownership.
A one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many relationship describes the multiplicity of an association.
Aggregation is a weak whole-part relationship: the part can exist independently of the whole.
Composition is a stronger ownership relationship: the whole controls the lifecycle or ownership of its parts as a design concept.
Java has no dedicated aggregation or composition keyword; these relationships are represented using object references and lifecycle rules.
In aggregation, a Department may refer to Professor objects that can exist independently of that department.
In composition, an Order may create and manage its OrderItem objects as part of its own lifecycle.
These terms describe design semantics, not something the Java compiler can infer from a field declaration alone.
Choose composition when an object should delegate work to contained collaborators instead of inheriting their implementation.

whyItExists.explanation: Object relationships describe how objects collaborate and whether one object owns or depends on another. Distinguishing the relationship helps communicate lifecycle and responsibility.
whyItExists.designProblemSolved: Without clearly modelling relationships, developers can create accidental ownership, unclear object lifecycles, and tightly coupled classes.
problemsWithoutConcept: It becomes unclear which object creates or owns another object.
Lifecycle responsibilities can be handled inconsistently.
The design may prevent independent reuse of objects that should exist separately.

basicExample.output:
Treating Asha
Ravi
Order item added
basicExample.beginnerNote: Java does not have special aggregation or composition keywords. These are design relationships expressed through references, construction, visibility, and lifecycle rules. Garbage collection also means composition does not automatically guarantee immediate destruction of a part. Arrays.asList is used here so the example also works on Java 8.

walkthrough.approach: Contrast three object relationship strengths in one program: association (`Doctor` uses `Patient`), aggregation (`Department` holds external `Professor`s), and composition (`Order` creates and owns `OrderItem`s).

steps.title: Association (collaborating peers)
steps.detail: Doctor.treat(Patient) accepts a Patient parameter for a single interaction; neither object owns the other.

steps.title: Aggregation (shared whole-part)
steps.detail: Department receives a List<Professor> created outside; the Professor exists independently of the Department.

steps.title: Composition (exclusive ownership)
steps.detail: Order encapsulates a private final List<OrderItem> and instantiates new OrderItem(name) internally inside addItem().

walkthrough.flow: doctor.treat(patient) prints 'Treating Asha'. Department wraps an externally created Professor('Ravi') and prints 'Ravi'. order.addItem('Book') constructs an internal OrderItem and prints 'Order item added'.
pitfalls: Looking for special Java keywords for aggregation vs. composition—both use standard object references; the difference is lifecycle ownership and encapsulation.

keyLines.note: Aggregation: Professor instances are created outside and passed in.
Composition: Order creates and exclusively owns its OrderItem instances.

concepts.howItWorksDetailed: Association is the general relationship where objects know about or use one another. Aggregation is a weaker whole-part relationship where the part has an independent lifecycle. Composition is stronger ownership: the whole controls creation or lifecycle of its parts by design. These meanings are design conventions, not enforced language-level relationship types.
concepts.interviewTip: Explain that Java has no keywords for aggregation vs. composition—the distinction is lifecycle ownership (whether the whole creates and exclusively owns its parts).

concepts.name: Constructor
concepts.definition: A special class member used to initialize a new object; it has the class name and no return type.
concepts.realWorldExample: new Employee("Asha") invokes a matching Employee constructor.
javaNotes: A constructor initializes a new object, has the same name as its class and has no return type, not even void.
Constructors can be overloaded, but they cannot be overridden or inherited.
If no constructor is declared, Java provides a default no-argument constructor; once any constructor is declared, that default is not generated.
If a constructor does not explicitly invoke this(...) or super(...), the compiler inserts an implicit no-argument super() call when applicable.
This implicit super() causes a compile-time error if the superclass has no accessible no-argument constructor.
This(...) invokes another constructor in the same class; super(...) invokes a superclass constructor. Either invocation must be the first statement in a constructor.
A constructor can be private, for example to control object creation in a utility class or singleton design.
Constructors are not inherited, and a subclass constructor must initialize its superclass portion.
Constructors cannot be abstract, static or final.
Instance field initializers and instance initializer blocks run as part of object initialization before the constructor body for that class.

whyItExists.explanation: A constructor establishes an object’s initial state at the moment it is created. It ensures required values can be supplied and invariants can be checked before the object is used.
whyItExists.designProblemSolved: Without constructors, callers may have to remember several setup calls after object creation. Forgetting one can leave the object incomplete or invalid.
problemsWithoutConcept: Objects may be created with missing required data.
Initialization logic may be duplicated at many call sites.
An object may be used before all required setup has happened.

basicExample.beginnerNote: If no constructor is declared, Java provides a default no-argument constructor. Once you declare any constructor, Java does not automatically add that no-argument constructor.

walkthrough.approach: Require mandatory object state (`name`, `age`) at creation time by declaring a parameterized constructor on `Employee`.

steps.title: Declare a parameterized constructor
steps.detail: Employee(String name, int age) matches the class name and has no return type, running automatically on new Employee(...).

steps.title: Disambiguate fields with this
steps.detail: this.name = name and this.age = age assign the constructor parameters to the new object's instance fields.

steps.title: Use the initialized instance
steps.detail: Calling employee.display() immediately after construction reads the initialized fields.

walkthrough.flow: new Employee('Neha', 28) allocates the Employee instance, initializes this.name = 'Neha' and this.age = 28 inside the constructor, and returns the reference. employee.display() prints 'Neha - 28'.
pitfalls: Writing name = name; without this., which assigns the parameter to itself and leaves the instance field at its default null value.
Calling new Employee() with no arguments after declaring Employee(String, int)—Java stops generating the default no-arg constructor once any constructor is declared.

keyLines.note: Constructor forces callers to supply name and age at instantiation.
this.name targets the instance field when shadowed by the parameter name.

concepts.howItWorksDetailed: When new is used, Java allocates and initializes the object’s fields to default values, then executes the selected constructor. A constructor may delegate to another constructor in the same class with this(...), or invoke a superclass constructor with super(...); either constructor invocation must be the first statement. Constructors are not inherited and cannot be overridden.
concepts.interviewTip: Highlight that constructors are never inherited or overridden, that `super(...)` or `this(...)` must be the first statement, and that declaring any constructor suppresses the default no-arg constructor.

concepts.name: Interface and Abstract Class
concepts.definition: Both define abstractions; interfaces primarily express contracts, while abstract classes can also share state and implementation.
concepts.realWorldExample: EmailSender and SmsSender implement NotificationSender; AbstractReport can share report workflow.
javaNotes: An interface defines a contract that a class can implement; an abstract class can define both shared state and shared implementation.
A class can implement multiple interfaces but can extend only one class.
An interface cannot be instantiated directly and does not have constructors or ordinary instance fields.
Interface fields are implicitly public, static and final, so they are constants.
Interface abstract methods are implicitly public; implementing methods must be public.
Interfaces can also declare default and static methods, and private helper methods (Java 9+) with method bodies.
An abstract class can have constructors, instance fields, instance methods with state, and methods with different access levels.
An abstract class may implement an interface without implementing every method, provided the class itself remains abstract.
If two implemented interfaces provide conflicting default methods, the implementing class must resolve the conflict by overriding the method.
Use an interface for a capability or contract that unrelated classes may share; use an abstract class when related classes need common state or base implementation.
Prefer programming to an interface type so implementations can be replaced and tested with less coupling.

whyItExists.explanation: Interfaces and abstract classes let developers define common contracts and shared structure without requiring callers to depend on one concrete implementation.
whyItExists.designProblemSolved: Without these abstractions, callers may depend directly on concrete classes, making implementations difficult to replace, test, or extend consistently.
problemsWithoutConcept: Callers become tightly coupled to a specific implementation.
Different classes may expose inconsistent method names for the same capability.
Shared behaviour may be copied instead of being defined once in a suitable base type.

basicExample.output:
Email: Interview reminder
SMS: Interview reminder
basicExample.beginnerNote: Use an interface when defining a capability or contract across potentially unrelated classes. Use an abstract class when related subclasses need shared instance state, constructors, or common implementation. A class can implement multiple interfaces but extend only one class.

walkthrough.approach: Define a `NotificationSender` interface contract and swap concrete implementations (`EmailSender`, `SmsSender`) behind the same reference variable.

steps.title: Declare the capability contract
steps.detail: NotificationSender declares void send(String message), which is implicitly public and abstract.

steps.title: Implement the contract in independent classes
steps.detail: EmailSender and SmsSender each implement NotificationSender with public void send(String).

steps.title: Swap implementations using the interface type
steps.detail: Main assigns EmailSender and then SmsSender to the same NotificationSender variable and invokes send().

walkthrough.flow: sender first references an EmailSender and prints 'Email: Interview reminder'. Reassigning sender = new SmsSender() and calling sender.send(...) dispatches to SmsSender.send() and prints 'SMS: Interview reminder'.
pitfalls: Forgetting the public modifier when implementing an interface method in a class—interface methods are implicitly public, so leaving off public makes the class method package-private and causes a compile error.

keyLines.note: Contract shared by all notification channels.
Implementing method must be declared public to match the interface visibility.

concepts.howItWorksDetailed: An interface defines a reference type and can contain abstract methods, constants, default methods, static methods, and private helper methods (depending on Java version). An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly and may contain constructors, instance fields, concrete methods, and abstract methods. A concrete subclass must implement inherited abstract methods unless it is also abstract.
concepts.interviewTip: Use an interface to define capabilities/contracts across potentially unrelated types, and an abstract class when closely related subclasses must share non-static state or template workflow.

conceptual.question: What is object-oriented programming (OOP)?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: OOP organizes software around objects that combine state and behaviour.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: It models domain entities and the responsibilities they perform. Its four commonly cited pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: A shopping application can model Customer, Product, Cart and Order as collaborating objects.

codeExample.output:
Asha is working
Ravi is working

walkthrough.approach: Model an `Employee` domain object that encapsulates state (`name`) with behavior (`work()`) and instantiate two independent objects.

steps.title: Encapsulate state inside the class
steps.detail: Employee declares private final String name so each object owns its own data.

steps.title: Initialize via constructor
steps.detail: Employee(String name) assigns the employee's name when new Employee(...) is called.

steps.title: Invoke behavior on each instance
steps.detail: e1.work() and e2.work() execute the same method body against each object's own name.

walkthrough.flow: Main creates two Employee instances ('Asha' and 'Ravi') and invokes work() on each, printing 'Asha is working' and 'Ravi is working'.
pitfalls: Writing procedural utility classes with only static methods and public fields instead of binding state and behavior together.

keyLines.note: Binds immutable state to each Employee instance.
Invokes behavior on the specific receiver object e1.

importantPoints: OOP organizes software around objects that combine state and behaviour.
It models domain entities and the responsibilities they perform. Its four commonly cited pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.
Java example to remember: class.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: What are the four pillars of OOP?
followUpQuestions.answer: The four pillars are encapsulation (bundling data with validating operations), abstraction (exposing contracts while hiding implementation details), inheritance (deriving specialized subtypes with `extends`), and polymorphism (substituting multiple implementations behind one contract). They complement one another rather than acting as a checklist every class must use.

walkthrough.approach: Combine an interface contract (abstraction), private state (encapsulation), contract implementation, and interface-typed dispatch (polymorphism) in one flow.

steps.title: Expose the abstraction
steps.detail: PaymentGateway declares pay(int) so callers know what operation exists without knowing how UPI or card networks work.

steps.title: Encapsulate provider state
steps.detail: UpiGateway keeps vpa private and final, initializing it through its constructor so external code cannot corrupt it.

steps.title: Dispatch polymorphically at runtime
steps.detail: Main holds a PaymentGateway reference pointing to a UpiGateway instance; calling gateway.pay(500) dynamically dispatches to UpiGateway.pay.

followUpQuestions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of OOP?
followUpQuestions.answer: OOP improves modularity, state safety, testability (via mockable interfaces), and domain alignment. Its trade-offs are extra indirection across small classes, heap allocation and pointer-chasing overhead compared to flat primitive arrays, and overengineering when a stateless function or Java `record` is enough.

conceptual.question: What is the difference between a class and an object?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: A class is a blueprint; an object is a runtime instance of that blueprint.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: A class declares the fields and methods its objects can have. Each object has its own instance state, while static members belong to the class.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: Employee defines name and salary; employee1 and employee2 are separate Employee objects.

Ravi is working

steps.title: Define the single class blueprint
steps.detail: class Employee declares what fields and methods every Employee instance will have.

steps.title: Create two runtime instances with new
steps.detail: new Employee('Asha') and new Employee('Ravi') allocate two distinct objects in heap memory.

steps.title: Observe independent state
steps.detail: Calling e1.work() and e2.work() shows that each object retains its own name.

walkthrough.flow: One Employee class definition produces two runtime instances on the heap. e1.work() prints 'Asha is working' and e2.work() prints 'Ravi is working'.
pitfalls: Confusing a reference variable (e1) with the heap object itself—multiple variables can point to the same object.

followUpQuestions.question: Can one class create multiple objects?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes. A class is defined once, and every `new` expression allocates a distinct object on the heap with its own copy of instance fields, while `static` fields are shared across all instances of that class.

walkthrough.approach: Contrast per-object instance fields (`label`) with class-level shared state (`static int totalCreated`) across multiple instantiations.

steps.title: Declare shared vs. per-instance state
steps.detail: totalCreated is marked static (one copy per class), whereas label is an instance field (one copy per object).

steps.title: Construct multiple instances
steps.detail: new Counter('First') and new Counter('Second') allocate two separate objects and increment the shared counter twice.

steps.title: Inspect both states
steps.detail: When printStatus() runs on c1 and c2, each prints its own distinct label alongside the shared totalCreated value of 2.

walkthrough.flow: Creating c1 sets c1.label = 'First' and increments Counter.totalCreated to 1. Creating c2 sets c2.label = 'Second' and increments Counter.totalCreated to 2. Both printStatus() calls read their own instance's label and the shared static totalCreated (2).
pitfalls: Accidentally marking an instance field static, which causes every object created from the class to overwrite the same shared value.

keyLines.note: Belongs to the Counter class metadata, not to individual instances.
Allocated separately inside every new Counter object.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Always pair 'yes, one class creates many objects' with the memory distinction: each instance gets its own instance fields, while `static` fields exist once per classloader.

followUpQuestions.question: Where are objects stored in Java?
followUpQuestions.answer: In standard JVM implementations, objects (and their instance fields) are allocated on the heap, while local reference variables live in the executing thread's stack frame. The JIT compiler may use escape analysis to scalar-replace short-lived non-escaping objects on the stack/registers as an internal optimization.

walkthrough.approach: Show that two local reference variables on the stack can point to the exact same Box object on the heap.

steps.title: Allocate object on the heap
steps.detail: new Box(10) allocates one Box instance on the heap and stores its reference in the local stack variable firstRef.

steps.title: Copy the reference value
steps.detail: Box secondRef = firstRef copies the reference handle, not the heap object. Both stack variables now alias the same heap instance.

steps.title: Mutate through one reference, observe through the other
steps.detail: Setting secondRef.value = 99 modifies the single shared heap object, so reading firstRef.value prints 99.

walkthrough.flow: main() creates one Box on the heap with value = 10. Assigning secondRef = firstRef points both stack variables to that single Box. Mutating secondRef.value updates the heap field to 99, which firstRef.value immediately sees.
pitfalls: Saying 'primitive variables are always on the stack'—primitive instance fields (like Box.value) live inside their enclosing object on the heap!

keyLines.note: firstRef is a local variable in main's stack frame; new Box(10) lives on the heap.
Copies only the reference handle—no second Box object is allocated.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Clarify a classic interview trap: local primitives live on the stack, but primitive *instance fields* live inside the object on the heap.

conceptual.question: Explain encapsulation in Java.

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Encapsulation protects an object's state by keeping fields private and exposing controlled operations.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: Methods validate changes and preserve business rules. It is more than generating getters and setters; the goal is to prevent invalid state and hide representation.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: A bank account exposes deposit() and withdraw() rather than a public balance field.

walkthrough.approach: Keep `BankAccount.balance` `private` and enforce validation rules inside the constructor and `deposit(double)` method.

steps.title: Hide the raw field
steps.detail: private double balance prevents callers from assigning invalid or negative numbers directly.

steps.title: Validate inside constructor and deposit()
steps.detail: Both constructor and deposit() throw IllegalArgumentException if the amount is invalid.

steps.title: Read state via getBalance()
steps.detail: getBalance() returns the current value without exposing mutable state.

walkthrough.flow: new BankAccount(100) initializes balance = 100.0 after validation. account.deposit(50) validates 50 > 0 and updates balance to 150.0, which getBalance() prints.
pitfalls: Adding an unvalidated setBalance(double) method, which breaks encapsulation by letting callers bypass deposit rules.

keyLines.note: Hides internal state from external classes.
Enforces positive-deposit invariant inside the mutator.

importantPoints: Encapsulation protects an object's state by keeping fields private and exposing controlled operations.
Methods validate changes and preserve business rules. It is more than generating getters and setters; the goal is to prevent invalid state and hide representation.

Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Is using getters and setters alone sufficient for encapsulation?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. Making fields `private` and auto-generating unrestricted public getters and setters only wraps field access in method syntax without protecting invariants. Real encapsulation exposes domain operations (like `deposit` and `withdraw`) that validate inputs and reject illegal state transitions.

walkthrough.approach: Contrast an anemically encapsulated class (private field + unrestricted setter) against a domain-encapsulated class (constructor + mutator validation).

steps.title: Expose the flaw in unrestricted setters
steps.detail: UnsafeAccount marks balance private, but setBalance(double) accepts any number, allowing callers to set -500.0.

steps.title: Guard construction invariants
steps.detail: SafeAccount validates openingBalance >= 0 in its constructor so an invalid instance can never exist.

steps.title: Replace raw setters with validated domain methods
steps.detail: deposit(double) enforces amount > 0 before mutating balance, centralizing the business rule inside the class.

walkthrough.flow: unsafe.setBalance(-500) directly overwrites UnsafeAccount.balance with -500.0 because no guard exists. SafeAccount(1000) passes constructor validation, and safe.deposit(200) passes the positive-amount check, adding 200 to produce 1200.0.
pitfalls: Auto-generating IDE getters and setters for every field—this leaks internal representation and scatters validation across callers.

keyLines.note: An unrestricted public setter defeats encapsulation even though balance is marked private.
Intention-revealing domain method enforces the invariant before state changes.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Say: 'Private fields + public setters is just syntax; encapsulation is invariant protection.' Mention replacing `setBalance()` with `deposit()`/`withdraw()`.

followUpQuestions.question: How does encapsulation improve maintainability?
followUpQuestions.answer: Encapsulation decouples callers from internal data representation and centralizes validation in one place. You can change how state is stored internally (for example, storing balance in integer paise/cents instead of `double`) without breaking or editing any caller that uses the public methods.

walkthrough.approach: Hide an internal representation change (`long balanceInPaise` instead of `double balance`) behind a stable public API (`deposit(double)` and `getBalance()`).

steps.title: Hide internal representation
steps.detail: BankAccount stores money internally as private long balanceInPaise to avoid floating-point drift, keeping the field invisible to callers.

steps.title: Preserve the external method contract
steps.detail: The constructor, deposit(double), and getBalance() still accept and return rupees as double, so Main needs zero changes.

steps.title: Centralize validation rules
steps.detail: Both the constructor and deposit() enforce non-negative/positive rules in one place rather than duplicating checks across callers.

walkthrough.flow: new BankAccount(100) converts 100 rupees to 10000 paise internally. account.deposit(50) validates 50 > 0 and adds 5000 paise. account.getBalance() divides 15000 by 100.0 and prints 150.0.
pitfalls: Exposing internal storage types in public fields—if balance were public double, switching to long paise or BigDecimal would break every caller.

keyLines.note: Internal representation uses long paise, completely hidden from external callers.
Translates internal state back to the public contract.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Give a concrete refactoring example: 'If `balance` is encapsulated, I can migrate internal storage from `double` to `BigDecimal` or integer paise without touching a single caller.'

conceptual.question: What is abstraction?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Abstraction exposes essential behaviour and hides implementation details.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: Callers depend on a contract rather than implementation steps. Java supports abstraction through interfaces and abstract classes.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: A caller invokes paymentService.pay() without knowing whether payment uses UPI or a card.

walkthrough.approach: Define an abstract `Shape` contract (`area()`) while hiding the geometry-specific formula inside the concrete `Circle` subclass.

steps.title: Declare the abstract contract
steps.detail: Shape declares abstract double area() so callers know every Shape can compute its area.

steps.title: Encapsulate Circle-specific formula
steps.detail: Circle stores private final double r and implements area() using Math.PI * r * r.

steps.title: Invoke the contract
steps.detail: new Circle(2).area() runs Circle's implementation after Shape's constructor initializes the base layer.

walkthrough.flow: new Circle(2) first runs Shape() ('Shape initialized'), sets r = 2.0, and computes area() > 0 ('true').
pitfalls: Attempting to instantiate an abstract class directly with new Shape().

keyLines.note: Exposes what a Shape can do without specifying how.
Concrete subclass supplies the hidden implementation detail.

importantPoints: Abstraction exposes essential behaviour and hides implementation details.
Callers depend on a contract rather than implementation steps. Java supports abstraction through interfaces and abstract classes.

followUpQuestions.question: Abstraction versus encapsulation?
followUpQuestions.answer: Abstraction is a design-level concern that hides *what happens behind an operation* by exposing a clean contract (interfaces/abstract classes). Encapsulation is an implementation-level boundary that hides *internal state representation* and protects invariants (private fields + validated methods).

walkthrough.approach: Show both concepts side by side in the same snippet: an interface providing abstraction for the caller, and a concrete class using encapsulation to protect its internal balance.

steps.title: Abstraction defines what the caller sees
steps.detail: PaymentGateway exposes only pay(int), hiding whether the payment uses a wallet balance, UPI, or a credit card API.

steps.title: Encapsulation protects how state is stored and mutated
steps.detail: WalletGateway keeps walletBalance private and validates that 0 < amount <= walletBalance inside pay(int).

steps.title: Caller interacts only with the abstraction
steps.detail: Main calls gateway.pay(400) without knowing walletBalance even exists.

walkthrough.flow: Main creates a WalletGateway (with walletBalance = 1000) referenced as PaymentGateway. Calling gateway.pay(400) dispatches to WalletGateway.pay, which validates the amount, subtracts 400 from private walletBalance, and prints 'Paid 400, remaining=600'.
pitfalls: Saying both simply 'hide things'—always specify that abstraction hides behavioral complexity via contracts, while encapsulation hides state and enforces invariants.

keyLines.note: Abstraction: exposes only the essential pay(int) contract.
Encapsulation: internal balance is hidden and guarded by validation in pay().

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Use the one-liner: 'Abstraction focuses on the outside view (what an object does via interfaces); encapsulation focuses on the inside view (how state is protected via private fields and validation).'

followUpQuestions.question: Can interfaces contain implemented methods?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes. Since Java 8, interfaces can declare `default` methods (overridable instance methods with a body) and `static` helper methods. Since Java 9, interfaces can also declare `private` and `private static` methods to share internal code between default methods without exposing helpers publicly.

walkthrough.approach: Demonstrate all three kinds of implemented interface methods in Java 17: a `static` utility method, a `default` method providing shared workflow, and a `private` helper method called by the default method.

steps.title: Declare the abstract contract
steps.detail: printBody(int) has no body, so implementing classes like UpiReceiptPrinter must implement it.

steps.title: Add a default method for evolving contracts
steps.detail: default void printReceipt(int) provides an inherited implementation that calls private formatHeader() and abstract printBody(amount).

steps.title: Use private and static interface helpers
steps.detail: private formatHeader() encapsulates helper logic inside the interface (Java 9+), while static isValidAmount(int) is called on the interface type.

walkthrough.flow: Main first calls ReceiptPrinter.isValidAmount(500), which returns true. It then calls printer.printReceipt(500), running the interface's default method: formatHeader() returns '=== RECEIPT ===', and printBody(500) dynamically dispatches to UpiReceiptPrinter.
pitfalls: Assuming default methods let interfaces hold mutable instance fields—interfaces still cannot have instance variables; all interface fields are implicitly public static final.

keyLines.note: default method provides a concrete instance implementation that subclasses inherit.
private interface method (Java 9+) shares helper code between default methods.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Mention why default methods were added in Java 8 (to add `Collection.stream()` and `Iterable.forEach()` without breaking existing implementations) and remember Java 9 `private` interface methods.

conceptual.question: Explain inheritance with an example.

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Inheritance lets a subclass extend a superclass using extends.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: The subclass inherits accessible members and can add or override eligible behaviour. It should represent a valid is-a relationship.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: SavingsAccount extends Account and adds interest calculation.

walkthrough.approach: Extend `Person` with `Employee` using `extends` and initialize inherited state via `super(name)`.

steps.title: Define shared state in Person
steps.detail: Person declares String name and initializes it in Person(String name).

steps.title: Derive Employee from Person
steps.detail: Employee extends Person inherits the accessible name field.

steps.title: Chain constructor and use inherited state
steps.detail: Employee(String) calls super(name), and introduce() prints the inherited name field.

walkthrough.flow: new Employee('Mira') calls super('Mira') to set Person.name = 'Mira', and introduce() prints 'Mira'.
pitfalls: Using inheritance between classes that do not have a genuine IS-A relationship.

keyLines.note: Establishes the IS-A inheritance relationship.
Delegates initialization of inherited state to the Person constructor.

The subclass inherits accessible members and can add or override eligible behaviour. It should represent a valid is-a relationship.

followUpQuestions.question: Does Java support multiple class inheritance?
followUpQuestions.answer: No, Java does not support multiple inheritance of classes (`class C extends A, B` is a compile-time error) to avoid conflicting instance state and constructor ambiguity (the diamond problem). However, a class can implement multiple interfaces (`class C implements A, B`) to inherit multiple type contracts.

walkthrough.approach: Show how a single Java class combines multiple capabilities by implementing two interfaces (`Auditable` and `Exportable`) without multiple class inheritance.

steps.title: Define orthogonal capability interfaces
steps.detail: Auditable and Exportable each define a focused contract with a default method and no mutable instance fields.

steps.title: Implement multiple interfaces in one class
steps.detail: Report implements both Auditable and Exportable, legally inheriting both contracts and their non-conflicting default methods.

steps.title: Invoke combined capabilities
steps.detail: Report.printSummary() calls both auditTag() and formatTag() without state ambiguity.

walkthrough.flow: new Report().printSummary() invokes auditTag() from Auditable ('AUDITED') and formatTag() from Exportable ('CSV'), printing 'AUDITED:CSV'.
pitfalls: Forgetting what happens if both interfaces define a default method with the exact same signature—the compiler forces the implementing class to override that method and resolve the conflict explicitly.

keyLines.note: A class can extend only one superclass, but can implement any number of interfaces.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Distinguish *multiple inheritance of state* (forbidden in Java classes) from *multiple inheritance of type/behavior* (supported via interfaces and default methods).

followUpQuestions.question: Why is composition often preferred?
followUpQuestions.answer: Composition (`HAS-A`) is preferred over inheritance (`IS-A`) because inheritance tightly couples a subclass to its superclass's internal implementation details (the fragile base-class problem) and locks the relationship at compile time. Composition keeps classes encapsulated and lets you swap collaborators at runtime.

walkthrough.approach: Compose a `Car` with an injected `Engine` interface collaborator rather than making `Car` extend a concrete `Engine` class.

steps.title: Define the collaborator contract
steps.detail: Engine declares start() so Car does not depend on any specific engine implementation.

steps.title: Hold the collaborator as a private field (HAS-A)
steps.detail: Car stores private final Engine engine and receives it via constructor injection.

steps.title: Delegate work instead of inheriting it
steps.detail: Car.start() forwards the call to engine.start(), allowing any Engine implementation (Petrol, Electric, Mock) to be plugged in.

walkthrough.flow: Main instantiates ElectricEngine and passes it into new Car(...). Calling car.start() delegates to engine.start(), which executes ElectricEngine.start() and prints 'Electric engine silent start'.
pitfalls: Extending a class just to reuse its helper methods (like java.util.Stack extending Vector), which leaks unwanted parent methods into your public API.

keyLines.note: Composition: Car holds a private Engine collaborator instead of extending Engine.
Delegation forwards only the intended operation without exposing Engine internals.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Cite `java.util.Stack extends Vector` or `Properties extends Hashtable` from the JDK standard library as famous real-world examples of why inheritance for code reuse breaks encapsulation.

conceptual.question: What is polymorphism?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Polymorphism lets one common type represent different concrete implementations.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: A superclass or interface reference can point to different objects. Overridden instance methods are selected according to the runtime object's class.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); uses the List contract with an ArrayList implementation.

walkthrough.approach: Reference a concrete `UpiPayment` object through its `Payment` interface type and invoke `p.pay()` via dynamic dispatch.

steps.title: Declare the shared interface
steps.detail: Payment declares void pay().

steps.title: Provide multiple implementations
steps.detail: CardPayment and UpiPayment each implement Payment.pay().

steps.title: Invoke through the common interface reference
steps.detail: Payment p = new UpiPayment(); p.pay() dynamically dispatches to UpiPayment.pay().

walkthrough.flow: The compiler verifies p.pay() against Payment. At runtime, the JVM inspects the actual object (UpiPayment) and prints 'UPI'.
pitfalls: Confusing compile-time reference type (which controls accessible methods) with runtime object type (which selects the overridden method body).

keyLines.note: Interface reference points to a concrete UpiPayment instance.
Dispatches at runtime to UpiPayment.pay().

importantPoints: Polymorphism lets one common type represent different concrete implementations.
A superclass or interface reference can point to different objects. Overridden instance methods are selected according to the runtime object's class.

followUpQuestions.question: Overloading versus overriding?
followUpQuestions.answer: Method overloading is compile-time polymorphism: methods in the same scope share a name but have different parameter lists, and the compiler picks the target signature using declared argument types. Method overriding is runtime polymorphism: a subclass replaces an inherited instance method with the same signature, and the JVM selects the implementation based on the actual heap object.

UPI override int: 100
Base double overload: 99.5

walkthrough.approach: Combine overloading (`process(int)` vs `process(double)`) and overriding (`UpiProcessor` overriding `process(int)`) in one trace to show how compile-time signature selection and runtime dispatch interact.

steps.title: Resolve the overload signature at compile time
steps.detail: For proc.process(100), the compiler selects process(int) on PaymentProcessor; for proc.process(99.5), it selects process(double).

steps.title: Dispatch to the actual object's override at runtime
steps.detail: At runtime, proc points to a UpiProcessor. Because UpiProcessor overrides process(int), proc.process(100) runs UpiProcessor.process(int).

steps.title: Fall back to inherited overload when not overridden
steps.detail: UpiProcessor does not override process(double), so proc.process(99.5) executes PaymentProcessor.process(double).

walkthrough.flow: The compiler binds proc.process(100) to the process(int) slot and proc.process(99.5) to the process(double) slot. At runtime on the UpiProcessor instance, the process(int) slot dispatches to UpiProcessor ('UPI override int: 100'), while process(double) runs the inherited base method ('Base double overload: 99.5').
pitfalls: Thinking overload resolution looks at the runtime object type of arguments—Java chooses overloads strictly at compile time using the declared reference types of the arguments.

keyLines.note: Overloads differ in parameter types (double vs int) and are chosen at compile time.
@Override replaces process(int) for runtime dispatch on UpiProcessor instances.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Walk through the two-phase rule: 'First, javac picks the method signature at compile time (overloading); second, the JVM picks the method body at runtime based on the heap object (overriding).'

followUpQuestions.question: What is dynamic method dispatch?
followUpQuestions.answer: Dynamic method dispatch is the runtime mechanism by which the JVM resolves a call to an overridden instance method (`invokevirtual` / `invokeinterface`) by looking up the actual class of the heap object rather than the compile-time type of the reference variable.

walkthrough.approach: Reassign the same `Payment` interface reference to two different concrete implementations (`UpiPayment` and `CardPayment`) and trace how `p.pay()` dispatches at runtime.

steps.title: Compile-time contract check
steps.detail: The compiler checks that pay() is declared on the reference type Payment and emits an invokeinterface bytecode instruction.

steps.title: First runtime dispatch
steps.detail: When p holds a UpiPayment instance, the JVM inspects p's runtime class pointer and invokes UpiPayment.pay(), printing 'UPI'.

steps.title: Second runtime dispatch after reassignment
steps.detail: After p = new CardPayment(), the exact same call site p.pay() inspects the new runtime object and invokes CardPayment.pay(), printing 'Card'.

walkthrough.flow: p first points to a UpiPayment object on the heap, so p.pay() prints 'UPI'. Reassigning p to new CardPayment() changes the heap target, so the second p.pay() prints 'Card'.
pitfalls: Assuming dynamic dispatch also applies to fields, static methods, or private methods—all three are bound statically at compile time using the declared reference type.

keyLines.note: Compile-time type is Payment, but runtime class is UpiPayment.
Reassigning p changes the runtime class without changing the caller expression p.pay().

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Explicitly state what dynamic dispatch does *not* cover: instance fields, `static` methods, `private` methods, and `final` methods are not dynamically dispatched.

conceptual.question: What are the four pillars of OOP?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: The four commonly cited pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: Encapsulation protects state; abstraction hides implementation details; inheritance models specialization; polymorphism enables interchangeable implementations.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: A payment interface hides provider details, while different implementations process payments differently.

walkthrough.approach: Illustrate how abstraction (`Payment` interface) and polymorphism (`CardPayment` vs `UpiPayment` implementations) work together.

steps.title: Abstraction defines the contract
steps.detail: Payment exposes pay() without tying callers to a payment rail.

steps.title: Implementations specialize behavior
steps.detail: CardPayment and UpiPayment implement Payment with distinct logic.

steps.title: Polymorphism selects the runtime behavior
steps.detail: Payment p = new UpiPayment(); p.pay() executes UpiPayment.pay().

walkthrough.flow: Main binds Payment p to a UpiPayment object and calls p.pay(), which dynamically dispatches to UpiPayment and prints 'UPI'.
pitfalls: Forgetting that encapsulation and inheritance/implementation complete the picture by protecting state and sharing contracts.

keyLines.note: Abstraction pillar: hides payment rail details behind pay().
Polymorphism pillar: one contract reference, interchangeable runtime objects.

importantPoints: The four commonly cited pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.
Encapsulation protects state; abstraction hides implementation details; inheritance models specialization; polymorphism enables interchangeable implementations.

Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Give a real-world example of each pillar.
followUpQuestions.answer: In an e-commerce checkout flow: (1) Encapsulation keeps `CardPayment.limit` private and validates `pay(amount)`; (2) Abstraction exposes a `PaymentMethod` interface hiding gateway details; (3) Inheritance lets `RewardCardPayment` extend `CardPayment` to add loyalty points; (4) Polymorphism lets `Main` call `method.pay(amount)` on any implementation.

walkthrough.approach: Demonstrate all four pillars in a single domain scenario (payment processing) so you can point to one cohesive example in an interview.

steps.title: Abstraction (PaymentMethod)
steps.detail: Defines the pay(int) contract so the caller in Main does not care how payments or rewards are processed.

steps.title: Encapsulation (CardPayment.limit)
steps.detail: Keeps limit private and deducts from it only after checking amount <= limit.

steps.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism (RewardCardPayment)
steps.detail: RewardCardPayment extends CardPayment, reuses super.pay(amount), and is invoked polymorphically via a PaymentMethod reference.

walkthrough.flow: Main holds a PaymentMethod reference pointing to a RewardCardPayment object. Calling method.pay(500) dynamically dispatches to RewardCardPayment.pay(500), which calls super.pay(500) to validate and deduct from private limit (printing 'Card paid: 500') and then prints 'Reward points: 50'.
pitfalls: Giving four disconnected textbook examples (Animal/Dog, Car/Engine, Shape/Circle, BankAccount) instead of one unified production domain like Checkout/Payments.

keyLines.note: Encapsulation: private field protects card credit limit.
Inheritance: specializes CardPayment and calls super.pay(amount).

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Use a single domain (like Payment/Checkout) to illustrate all four pillars in 30 seconds—it sounds much more senior than switching between `Animal`, `Shape`, and `Car`.

followUpQuestions.question: Are association and composition OOP pillars?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. The four OOP pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism. Association, aggregation, and composition are object relationship and collaboration patterns (`USES-A` and `HAS-A`) that describe how objects reference each other and manage lifecycles.

walkthrough.approach: Contrast composition (`Car` owns its `Engine` lifecycle) with association (`Car` collaborates with an independent `Driver` passed to `drive()`).

steps.title: Model strong ownership with composition
steps.detail: Car instantiates and owns private final Engine engine internally; the Engine does not exist outside the Car.

steps.title: Model collaboration with association
steps.detail: Driver is created independently in Main and passed into car.drive(driver); Car uses Driver without owning its lifecycle.

walkthrough.flow: new Car() constructs its internal Engine. Main creates Driver('Asha') and calls car.drive(driver), which delegates to engine.start() ('Engine started') and reads driver.name ('Asha is driving').
pitfalls: Listing composition or association as one of the 'four pillars'—keep the four pillars distinct and frame association/aggregation/composition as structural relationship patterns.

keyLines.note: Composition (HAS-A): Car creates and exclusively owns its Engine instance.
Association (USES-A): Car collaborates with an external Driver without owning it.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Clarify that while composition is not one of the four textbook pillars, 'favor object composition over class inheritance' (Gang of Four) is one of the most important practical OOP design rules.

conceptual.question: What is the difference between abstraction and encapsulation?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Abstraction hides implementation complexity; encapsulation controls access to internal state and representation.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: Abstraction focuses on what is exposed to a caller. Encapsulation bundles data and behaviour and protects the object's invariants.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: A car's start() operation is an abstraction; private account balance with validated methods is encapsulation.

walkthrough.approach: Combine abstraction (`abstract class Shape` with `abstract double area()`) and encapsulation (`private final double r` in `Circle`) in one hierarchy.

steps.title: Expose the abstract operation
steps.detail: Shape declares abstract double area(), hiding geometry formulas from callers.

steps.title: Encapsulate the radius field
steps.detail: Circle marks private final double r so external code cannot mutate radius directly.

steps.title: Compute area through the public contract
steps.detail: new Circle(2).area() initializes Shape, sets r = 2, and returns a positive area.

walkthrough.flow: new Circle(2) runs Shape() ('Shape initialized'), initializes private r = 2, and evaluates area() > 0 ('true').
pitfalls: Treating abstraction and encapsulation as synonyms—abstraction hides behavioral complexity via contracts, while encapsulation hides internal state.

keyLines.note: Abstraction: callers only need to know area() exists.
Encapsulation: internal radius representation is private and immutable.

importantPoints: Abstraction hides implementation complexity; encapsulation controls access to internal state and representation.
Abstraction focuses on what is exposed to a caller. Encapsulation bundles data and behaviour and protects the object's invariants.
Java example to remember: abstract.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Can abstraction exist without encapsulation?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes, a type can define an abstraction (such as an interface contract) while its implementation fails to encapsulate its internal state (for example, by exposing `public` mutable fields). However, without encapsulation, callers can bypass the abstraction's contract and corrupt the object's state directly.

walkthrough.approach: Define a clean abstraction (`CounterService`), then show how an unencapsulated implementation (`public int count`) allows callers to corrupt state behind the abstraction's back.

steps.title: Define the abstraction
steps.detail: CounterService declares increment(), abstracting the counting operation.

steps.title: Break encapsulation in the implementation
steps.detail: LeakyCounter declares public int count = 0 instead of private, exposing raw state.

steps.title: Observe state corruption
steps.detail: Code with a LeakyCounter reference sets raw.count = -999 directly, so calling service.increment() produces -998 instead of a valid positive count.

walkthrough.flow: Main creates LeakyCounter, corrupts raw.count = -999 directly through the public field, and then calls service.increment() through the CounterService abstraction, resulting in -998.
pitfalls: Assuming that implementing an interface automatically encapsulates a class—you must still mark implementation fields private and guard all mutations.

keyLines.note: Provides abstraction by exposing only increment().
Breaks encapsulation, letting callers bypass increment() and set -999.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Summarize the synergy: 'Abstraction defines the contract boundary; encapsulation enforces that callers can only change state through that boundary.'

followUpQuestions.question: Which access modifiers help encapsulation?
followUpQuestions.answer: Java provides four access levels from most restrictive to broadest: `private` (same class only), package-private/default (same package), `protected` (same package plus subclasses in any package), and `public` (everywhere). Encapsulation relies primarily on `private` for fields/helpers and package-private/`public` for controlled entry points.

walkthrough.approach: Declare fields with `private`, package-private, and `protected` visibility on `Account` and expose the `private` state only through a `public` verification method.

steps.title: Hide sensitive state with private
steps.detail: private int pin = 1234 prevents Main or any other class from reading or overwriting the PIN directly.

steps.title: Scope package and subclass fields
steps.detail: branch (package-private) and tier (protected) are accessible within the same package.

steps.title: Expose a public verification behavior
steps.detail: public boolean verifyPin(int) checks the PIN internally and returns only a boolean result.

walkthrough.flow: Main creates Account, reads package-accessible branch ('Mumbai') and protected tier ('Gold'), and calls acc.verifyPin(1234) to check the private pin field, printing 'Mumbai | Gold | true'.
pitfalls: Forgetting that protected in Java ALSO grants access to any class in the same package, not just subclasses.

keyLines.note: Restricts direct access strictly to the Account class body.
Exposes controlled behavior without leaking the private pin value.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Mention the four levels in order (`private` -> package-private -> `protected` -> `public`) and point out the common trap that `protected` is *less* restrictive than package-private.
