conceptual.question: What is method overloading?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Overloading declares methods with the same name but different parameter lists.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: The compiler selects an applicable overload using argument types and overload-resolution rules. Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: Calculator can define add(int,int) and add(double,double).

walkthrough.approach: Overload `Calculator.add` with `(int, int)` and `(double, double)` parameter lists so the compiler binds each call using argument types.

steps.title: Declare overloaded methods
steps.detail: Calculator defines int add(int, int) and double add(double, double).

steps.title: Call with int literals
steps.detail: c.add(2, 3) matches add(int, int) at compile time and returns 5.

steps.title: Call with double literals
steps.detail: c.add(2.5, 3.0) matches add(double, double) at compile time and returns 5.5.

walkthrough.flow: javac resolves c.add(2, 3) to add(int, int) -> 5, and c.add(2.5, 3.0) to add(double, double) -> 5.5.
pitfalls: Attempting to overload methods by changing only the return type while keeping parameter types identical.

keyLines.note: Selected at compile time when arguments are (int, int).
Selected at compile time when arguments are (double, double).

importantPoints: Overloading declares methods with the same name but different parameter lists.
The compiler selects an applicable overload using argument types and overload-resolution rules. Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads.
Java example to remember: overload.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Can methods be overloaded by changing only return type?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. Method overloading requires a different parameter list (arity, parameter types, or parameter type order). Because callers can invoke a method and ignore its return value (for example, `calc.add(2, 3);`), the compiler cannot use return type alone to disambiguate which method to call.

walkthrough.approach: Distinguish overloaded methods by their parameter types (`(int, int)` vs `(double, double)`) rather than return type alone.

steps.title: Define distinct parameter signatures
steps.detail: In Java, a method's overload signature consists only of the method name and parameter types—return type is not part of the signature.

steps.title: Bind int arguments to add(int, int)
steps.detail: c.add(2, 3) passes two int literals, so javac selects add(int, int) at compile time.

steps.title: Bind double arguments to add(double, double)
steps.detail: c.add(2.5, 3.0) passes double literals, so javac selects add(double, double).

walkthrough.flow: At compile time, javac resolves c.add(2, 3) to Calculator.add(int, int) -> 5, and c.add(2.5, 3.0) to Calculator.add(double, double) -> 5.5.
pitfalls: Declaring int add(int a, int b) and double add(int a, int b) in the same class—javac fails with 'method add(int,int) is already defined in class Calculator'.

keyLines.note: Method signature is add(int, int); return type int is excluded from signature matching.
Valid overload because the parameter types (double, double) differ.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Give the exact compiler reason: 'In Java's grammar, you can call `add(2, 3);` as a standalone statement without assigning the result, so the compiler has no return-type context at the call site.'

followUpQuestions.question: Can static methods be overloaded?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes. `static` methods can be overloaded just like instance methods as long as their parameter lists differ. The compiler resolves which `static` overload to invoke at compile time based on the argument types.

walkthrough.approach: Declare three `static` `add` overloads on `Calculator` with different parameter types and counts, and resolve each call at compile time.

steps.title: Overload by parameter types
steps.detail: static int add(int, int) and static double add(double, double) differ in parameter types.

steps.title: Overload by parameter count (arity)
steps.detail: static int add(int, int, int) accepts three int parameters.

steps.title: Invoke directly on the class name
steps.detail: Main calls Calculator.add(...) without instantiating Calculator; javac binds each call to its matching static signature.

walkthrough.flow: Calculator.add(10, 20) calls add(int, int) and prints 30; Calculator.add(10.5, 20.5) calls add(double, double) and prints 31.0; Calculator.add(10, 20, 30) calls add(int, int, int) and prints 60.
pitfalls: Confusing static method overloading (allowed, resolved at compile time) with static method overriding (not possible—redeclaring a static method in a subclass hides it rather than overriding it).

keyLines.note: Two-parameter int static overload.
Three-parameter int static overload.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Answer immediately: 'Static methods can be overloaded, but they cannot be overridden (they are hidden).'

conceptual.question: What is method overriding?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Overriding occurs when a subclass provides a compatible implementation of an inherited instance method.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: Runtime dispatch selects the override based on the actual object. An override cannot reduce visibility or broaden checked exceptions beyond Java's rules.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: Dog overrides Animal.sound(); an Animal reference to Dog invokes Dog.sound().

walkthrough.approach: Override `Animal.sound()` in `Dog` and invoke `a.sound()` on an `Animal` reference pointing to a `Dog` instance.

steps.title: Declare base method in Animal
steps.detail: Animal defines void sound().

steps.title: Override in Dog with @Override
steps.detail: Dog provides its own void sound() implementation that prints 'bark'.

steps.title: Dispatch dynamically at runtime
steps.detail: Animal a = new Dog(); a.sound() selects Dog.sound() based on the heap object.

walkthrough.flow: Main upcasts new Dog() to Animal a. Calling a.sound() dynamically dispatches to Dog.sound() and prints 'bark'.
pitfalls: Narrowing access visibility or broadening checked exceptions in the overriding method, which causes a compile-time error.

keyLines.note: Verifies at compile time that Dog.sound() overrides Animal.sound().
Upcast reference; runtime object is Dog.

importantPoints: Overriding occurs when a subclass provides a compatible implementation of an inherited instance method.
Runtime dispatch selects the override based on the actual object. An override cannot reduce visibility or broaden checked exceptions beyond Java's rules.
Java example to remember: override.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Can private methods be overridden?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. A `private` method is invisible outside its declaring class and is not inherited by subclasses. If a subclass declares a method with the same name and parameters, it is a brand-new, independent method—not an override—and adding `@Override` to it causes a compile-time error.

walkthrough.approach: Trace what happens when `Parent.trigger()` calls a `private void secret()` method while the runtime object is a `Child` that defines its own `void secret()`.

steps.title: Declare a private method in Parent
steps.detail: private void secret() is bound statically to Parent at compile time because private methods are never inherited.

steps.title: Declare a same-named method in Child
steps.detail: Child.secret() is a separate method, not an override of Parent.secret().

steps.title: Call trigger() on a Child instance
steps.detail: When p.trigger() executes, secret() inside Parent resolves strictly to Parent.secret(), printing 'Parent secret'.

walkthrough.flow: Main creates new Child() and calls p.trigger(). Inside Parent.trigger(), the call to secret() uses non-virtual dispatch bound to Parent.secret(), printing 'Parent secret' even though the runtime object is Child.
pitfalls: Assuming Child.secret() overrides Parent.secret() and will be called when Parent.trigger() runs on a Child instance.

keyLines.note: Private method is not inherited and cannot be dynamically dispatched.
Independent method in Child; putting @Override here would fail compilation.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Explain that `private` methods use static binding (`invokespecial` / direct call), so even if a parent method calls `this.secret()` on a child object, the parent's `private` method runs.

followUpQuestions.question: What does @Override do?
followUpQuestions.answer: `@Override` is a compile-time annotation (`RetentionPolicy.SOURCE`) that instructs `javac` to verify the annotated method actually overrides an accessible superclass method or implements an interface method. It catches typos in method names or parameter types at compile time instead of silently creating an overload.

walkthrough.approach: Annotate `Dog.sound()` with `@Override` so the compiler verifies the signature against `Animal.sound()` before runtime dispatch.

steps.title: Define the superclass signature
steps.detail: Animal declares void sound() with no parameters.

steps.title: Guard the subclass method with @Override
steps.detail: javac checks that Dog's superclass or implemented interfaces declare an accessible sound() method with the exact signature.

steps.title: Dispatch at runtime
steps.detail: a.sound() invokes Dog.sound() and prints 'bark'.

walkthrough.flow: At compile time, @Override confirms Dog.sound() overrides Animal.sound(). At runtime, Animal a = new Dog(); a.sound() dispatches to Dog.sound() and prints 'bark'.
pitfalls: Omitting @Override when overriding equals(Object)—if you accidentally write public boolean equals(User other), you overload instead of overriding Object.equals(Object) without any compiler error!

keyLines.note: Compile-time safety check that fails compilation if the method signature does not match a supertype method.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Give the classic bug `@Override` prevents: writing `equals(MyClass o)` instead of `equals(Object o)`, which silently overloads `equals` and breaks `HashMap`/`HashSet` lookups.

conceptual.question: Overloading versus overriding: what is the difference?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Overloading changes the parameter list and is resolved at compile time; overriding replaces inherited instance behaviour and uses runtime dispatch.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: Overloading is commonly called compile-time polymorphism. Overriding is the main form of runtime polymorphism.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: Calculator overloads add(); Dog overrides Animal.sound().

walkthrough.approach: Demonstrate compile-time overload resolution on `Calculator.add` and contrast it with runtime override dispatch.

steps.title: Define distinct parameter lists for overloading
steps.detail: Calculator defines add(int, int) and add(double, double).

steps.title: Bind calls at compile time
steps.detail: javac binds c.add(2, 3) and c.add(2.5, 3.0) using the compile-time types of the arguments.

walkthrough.flow: c.add(2, 3) executes add(int, int) and prints 5; c.add(2.5, 3.0) executes add(double, double) and prints 5.5.
pitfalls: Thinking overloaded methods are chosen at runtime based on the actual object types of the arguments.

keyLines.note: Compile-time overload for int arguments.
Compile-time overload for double arguments.

importantPoints: Overloading changes the parameter list and is resolved at compile time; overriding replaces inherited instance behaviour and uses runtime dispatch.
Overloading is commonly called compile-time polymorphism. Overriding is the main form of runtime polymorphism.
Java example to remember: overload.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Can constructors be overloaded?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes, a class can overload constructors by declaring multiple constructors with different parameter lists. Constructors are never inherited or overridden; each constructor initializes its own class layer after chaining to another constructor via `this(...)` or to the superclass constructor via `super(...)`.

walkthrough.approach: Trace constructor overloading (`Child()` delegating to `Child(String)` via `this(...)`) together with superclass constructor chaining (`super()`).

steps.title: Invoke no-arg subclass constructor
steps.detail: new Child() calls Child(), which delegates to the overloaded constructor Child(String) using this('child').

steps.title: Chain to superclass constructor first
steps.detail: Child(String) executes super() as its first statement, running Base() and printing 'base' before subclass body code runs.

steps.title: Complete subclass constructor body
steps.detail: Control returns to Child(String), which prints 'child'.

walkthrough.flow: new Child() -> Child() -> this('child') -> Child(String) -> super() -> Base() prints 'base' -> Child(String) prints 'child'.
pitfalls: Attempting to call both this(...) and super(...) in the same constructor body—both must be the first statement, so a constructor can use one or the other, never both.

keyLines.note: Delegates to the overloaded constructor in the same class.
Initializes the Base layer before Child's body executes.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Point out that constructor overloading uses `this(...)` to avoid duplicating initialization logic across constructors, while `super(...)` initializes the parent layer.

followUpQuestions.question: Can static methods be overridden?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. `static` methods belong to the class rather than to individual object instances, so they are hidden, not overridden. When a `static` method is invoked through a reference variable, the compiler selects the method using the variable's declared compile-time type, ignoring the runtime object.

walkthrough.approach: Trace a `Parent` reference pointing to a `Child` instance when accessing a hidden `static` field and calling a hidden `static` method.

steps.title: Declare static members in both Parent and Child
steps.detail: Child.type and Child.print() hide Parent.type and Parent.print() instead of overriding them.

steps.title: Upcast Child to a Parent reference
steps.detail: Parent ref = new Child() gives ref a compile-time type of Parent and a runtime object of Child.

steps.title: Resolve static members at compile time
steps.detail: Both ref.type and ref.print() are bound by javac to Parent.type and Parent.print() based on ref's declared type.

walkthrough.flow: Even though new Child() is allocated, ref has compile-time type Parent. javac resolves ref.type to Parent.type ('Parent') and ref.print() to Parent.print() ('Parent').
pitfalls: Calling static methods on an instance variable (ref.print())—always call static methods on the class name (Parent.print()) so readers aren't misled into expecting dynamic dispatch.

keyLines.note: Hides Parent.print(); adding @Override here would cause a compile-time error.
Resolved at compile time using ref's declared type (Parent), not the runtime Child instance.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Mention bytecode: `static` methods compile to `invokestatic` bound to the declared class type at compile time, whereas overridden instance methods compile to `invokevirtual`.

conceptual.question: What is a constructor in Java?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: A constructor initializes a new object and has the same name as its class, with no return type.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: Constructors can be overloaded but are not inherited or overridden. Java supplies an implicit no-argument constructor only when no constructor is declared.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: new User("Ravi") invokes a matching constructor.

walkthrough.approach: Show how constructors run automatically during `new Child()`, chaining from `Child()` to `Base()` via `super()`.

steps.title: Define superclass constructor
steps.detail: Base() initializes the Base layer and prints 'base'.

steps.title: Chain from subclass constructor
steps.detail: Child() calls super() as its first statement before printing 'child'.

steps.title: Trigger construction with new
steps.detail: new Child() runs Base() first and Child() second.

walkthrough.flow: new Child() enters Child(), chains to Base() via super() ('base'), and completes Child() ('child').
pitfalls: Adding a return type like void Base()—that turns the constructor into an ordinary method that does not run on new Base()!

keyLines.note: Constructor name matches the class and has no return type.
Invokes the superclass constructor as the first statement.

importantPoints: A constructor initializes a new object and has the same name as its class, with no return type.
Constructors can be overloaded but are not inherited or overridden. Java supplies an implicit no-argument constructor only when no constructor is declared.
Java example to remember: constructor-call.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Is a constructor inherited?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. Constructors are tightly bound to creating an instance of their exact declaring class and are never inherited by subclasses. A subclass must define its own constructors (or rely on its own default no-arg constructor) and chain to a superclass constructor via `super(...)`.

walkthrough.approach: Trace how `Child()` invokes `Base()` through `super()` rather than inheriting `Base()` as a constructor of `Child`.

steps.title: Declare the superclass constructor
steps.detail: Base() initializes the Base portion of the object and prints 'base'.

steps.title: Chain from Child() using super()
steps.detail: Child() explicitly calls super() as its first statement to run Base() before running Child's own constructor body.

steps.title: Observe top-down initialization order
steps.detail: new Child() runs Base() first and Child() second.

walkthrough.flow: new Child() enters Child(), which immediately invokes super() -> Base(), printing 'base'. Control returns to Child(), which prints 'child'.
pitfalls: Assuming that if Parent defines Parent(String name), Child automatically gets Child(String name)—it does not; you must explicitly write Child(String name) { super(name); }.

keyLines.note: Invokes the superclass constructor; Base() is chained, not inherited.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Give the practical proof that constructors aren't inherited: if `Parent` only has `Parent(String name)`, you cannot call `new Child("Asha")` unless `Child` explicitly declares `Child(String name)`.

followUpQuestions.question: What is a default constructor?
followUpQuestions.answer: A default constructor is the no-argument constructor that the Java compiler automatically generates *only* when a class declares zero constructors of its own. It has the same access modifier as the class and contains a single `super();` call. Once you write any constructor (even a parameterized one), the compiler stops generating the default constructor.

walkthrough.approach: Compare a class that relies on the compiler-synthesized default constructor (`AutoDefault`) with a class that declares an explicit no-argument constructor (`ExplicitNoArg`).

steps.title: Rely on the compiler-generated default constructor
steps.detail: AutoDefault declares no constructors, so javac generates AutoDefault() { super(); }, leaving count at its default value 0.

steps.title: Write an explicit no-arg constructor
steps.detail: ExplicitNoArg declares ExplicitNoArg() and sets count = 10.

steps.title: Instantiate both classes
steps.detail: new AutoDefault().count prints 0, while new ExplicitNoArg().count prints 10.

walkthrough.flow: new AutoDefault() runs the compiler-generated default constructor and leaves count = 0. new ExplicitNoArg() runs the custom no-arg constructor and sets count = 10.
pitfalls: Adding a parameterized constructor (like User(String name)) to a JPA entity or Jackson DTO and forgetting that doing so removes the default no-arg constructor required by reflection frameworks.

keyLines.note: Has no explicit constructor, so javac synthesizes a default no-arg constructor.
Explicit no-argument constructor written by the developer.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Mention why this matters in Spring/Hibernate/Jackson: adding a parameterized constructor removes the implicit default constructor, which can break reflection-based deserialization unless you also add an explicit no-arg constructor.

conceptual.question: Explain this and super.

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: this refers to the current object; super is used to access superclass members or invoke a superclass constructor.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: this() chains to another constructor in the same class. super() invokes a superclass constructor. An explicit constructor invocation must be first.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: this.name = name assigns the current object's field; super.display() invokes the superclass implementation.

walkthrough.approach: Demonstrate all four uses of `this` and `super` in one program: constructor chaining (`this("Asha")` and `super(name)`) and member disambiguation (`this.role` vs `super.role`).

steps.title: Chain constructors in the same class with this(...)
steps.detail: Employee() calls this('Asha') to delegate to Employee(String name).

steps.title: Chain to the superclass constructor with super(...)
steps.detail: Employee(String name) calls super(name) to run Person(String name).

steps.title: Disambiguate shadowed fields with this.role and super.role
steps.detail: printRoles() reads Employee's field via this.role and Person's hidden field via super.role.

walkthrough.flow: new Employee() calls this('Asha') -> super('Asha') prints 'Person: Asha'. Calling printRoles() prints 'Employee / Person'.
pitfalls: Trying to place both this(...) and super(...) inside the same constructor body—only one can be the first statement.

keyLines.note: Delegates to another constructor in the same class.
Invokes the superclass constructor.
Distinguishes current-class vs superclass members.

importantPoints: this refers to the current object; super is used to access superclass members or invoke a superclass constructor.
this() chains to another constructor in the same class. super() invokes a superclass constructor. An explicit constructor invocation must be first.
Java example to remember: polymorphism.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Can this() and super() both be called in the same constructor?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. Both `this(...)` and `super(...)` must be the very first statement in a constructor body, so a single constructor cannot contain both calls. Instead, one constructor calls `this(...)` to delegate to another constructor in the same class, and that target constructor calls `super(...)`.

walkthrough.approach: Chain `Child()` to `Child(String)` using `this(...)`, and let `Child(String)` invoke `super()` so the superclass constructor runs exactly once.

steps.title: Delegate within the same class using this(...)
steps.detail: Child() calls this('child') as its first statement instead of calling super().

steps.title: Invoke the superclass constructor in the target constructor
steps.detail: Child(String msg) calls super() as its first statement, initializing Base.

steps.title: Run constructor bodies in order
steps.detail: Base() prints 'base', and then Child(String) prints 'child'.

walkthrough.flow: new Child() enters Child(), chains to Child('child') via this('child'), chains to Base() via super() (printing 'base'), and finishes Child('child') (printing 'child').
pitfalls: Writing super(); followed by this('child'); in the same constructor—javac rejects it because the second call is no longer the first statement, and allowing both would initialize the superclass twice.

keyLines.note: First statement in Child(); delegates to Child(String).
First statement in Child(String); initializes Base.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Explain *why* Java forbids calling both in one constructor: if a constructor called `super()` and then `this()`, the target constructor would also call `super()`, initializing the superclass twice on the same object!

followUpQuestions.question: Can super directly access a private parent field?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. `private` fields belong strictly to the superclass and are not accessible via `super.fieldName` in a subclass. To initialize or read a `private` superclass field, the subclass must call an accessible (`protected` or `public`) superclass constructor (`super(...)`) or accessor method (`super.getField()`).

walkthrough.approach: Initialize a `private` superclass field through `super(secret)` and read it in the subclass via a `protected` superclass method.

steps.title: Keep superclass state private
steps.detail: Parent declares private final String secret so even subclasses cannot access super.secret directly.

steps.title: Initialize via super(secret)
steps.detail: Child(String) passes the value up to Parent(String) using super(secret).

steps.title: Read via a protected accessor
steps.detail: Child.print() calls super.readSecret(), which is protected and allowed to return secret.

walkthrough.flow: new Child('vault-42') passes 'vault-42' to Parent(String) via super(secret). Calling print() invokes super.readSecret() and prints 'vault-42'.
pitfalls: Thinking super bypasses private access control—private means private to the declaring class, even for subclasses.

keyLines.note: Exists inside every Child object on the heap, but cannot be accessed as super.secret.
Accesses the private parent state through a protected parent method.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Make a sharp distinction: a subclass *contains* the memory for its parent's `private` fields on the heap, but it cannot *name* them directly—it must go through `super(...)` or parent methods.

conceptual.question: What is an abstract class?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly and can contain abstract and concrete methods.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: It can have constructors and instance fields. It is useful when related subclasses share state or common implementation while completing some behaviour.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: AbstractReport shares header generation and requires subclasses to implement body generation.

walkthrough.approach: Combine a constructor and an `abstract` method inside `abstract class Shape`, and complete the implementation in `Circle`.

steps.title: Declare abstract base class
steps.detail: Shape defines a constructor Shape() and an abstract method double area().

steps.title: Implement the abstract method in Circle
steps.detail: Circle extends Shape, stores radius r, and implements area().

steps.title: Instantiate the concrete subclass
steps.detail: new Circle(2) runs Shape() first, then Circle(2), and area() computes the circle area.

walkthrough.flow: new Circle(2) invokes Shape() ('Shape initialized'), initializes r = 2, and evaluates area() > 0 ('true').
pitfalls: Trying to instantiate Shape directly with new Shape().

keyLines.note: Cannot be instantiated directly; can have constructors and state.
Must be implemented by concrete subclasses.

importantPoints: An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly and can contain abstract and concrete methods.
It can have constructors and instance fields. It is useful when related subclasses share state or common implementation while completing some behaviour.

followUpQuestions.question: Can an abstract class have a constructor?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes. An abstract class can declare constructors. Although you cannot call `new AbstractClass()` directly, its constructor executes whenever a concrete subclass is instantiated (via `super(...)`) to initialize shared fields and enforce superclass invariants.
followUpQuestions.output:
Payment constructor
UPI constructor
Payment through UPI

walkthrough.approach: Trace constructor chaining when instantiating a concrete subclass (`UpiPayment`) of an abstract superclass (`Payment`).

steps.title: Declare a constructor in the abstract class
steps.detail: Payment() initializes the abstract base layer and prints 'Payment constructor'.

steps.title: Implicitly chain from the subclass constructor
steps.detail: UpiPayment() has an implicit super() call as its first statement, which invokes Payment() before UpiPayment's body runs.

steps.title: Invoke the implemented abstract method
steps.detail: payment.pay() dispatches at runtime to UpiPayment.pay().

walkthrough.flow: new UpiPayment() invokes UpiPayment(), which first calls super() -> Payment() ('Payment constructor'), then finishes UpiPayment() ('UPI constructor'). Calling payment.pay() prints 'Payment through UPI'.
pitfalls: Confusing interfaces (which cannot have constructors because they hold no instance fields) with abstract classes (which always have a constructor, explicit or compiler-generated).

keyLines.note: Abstract class constructor; runs via super() during subclass instantiation.
Implicitly calls super() on its first line before printing 'UPI constructor'.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Explain the practical reason abstract classes have constructors: 'If an abstract class has `private final` fields, a constructor is the only place subclasses can initialize them via `super(...)`.'

followUpQuestions.question: Can it have no abstract methods?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes. A class can be declared `abstract` without declaring any `abstract` methods. Doing so prevents callers from instantiating the base class directly (`new Base()` is a compile error) while allowing subclasses to inherit its concrete helper methods and fields.

walkthrough.approach: Declare `BaseEntity` as `abstract` with only concrete members so it cannot be instantiated on its own, then instantiate its concrete `OrderEntity` subclass.

steps.title: Mark the base class abstract with zero abstract methods
steps.detail: BaseEntity provides id storage, a constructor, and getId(), but abstract forbids new BaseEntity(101L).

steps.title: Extend with a concrete domain class
steps.detail: OrderEntity extends BaseEntity and forwards id to super(id) without needing to implement any abstract methods.

steps.title: Instantiate the concrete subclass
steps.detail: Main creates new OrderEntity(101L) and calls the inherited getId() method.

walkthrough.flow: new OrderEntity(101L) chains to BaseEntity(101L) and sets id = 101. Calling order.getId() returns 101.
pitfalls: Thinking the compiler requires at least one abstract method inside an abstract class—the reverse is the rule: a class with an abstract method *must* be abstract, but an abstract class needs *zero* abstract methods.

keyLines.note: Prevents direct instantiation even though every method inside is concrete.
Concrete subclass inherits getId() without overriding anything.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Remember the one-way rule: 'Any class with an `abstract` method must be `abstract`, but an `abstract` class does not need any `abstract` methods.'

conceptual.question: What is an interface?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: An interface defines a contract that implementing classes agree to provide.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: A class can implement multiple interfaces. Modern Java interfaces can contain abstract, default, static and private methods.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: PaymentGateway can be implemented by UpiGateway and CardGateway.

walkthrough.approach: Implement two interfaces (`A` and `B`) in class `C` and resolve their conflicting `default void show()` methods using `A.super.show()`.

steps.title: Define contracts with default methods
steps.detail: Interfaces A and B both declare default void show().

steps.title: Implement multiple interfaces in C
steps.detail: class C implements A, B adopts both contracts.

steps.title: Resolve default method conflict explicitly
steps.detail: C overrides public void show() and delegates to A.super.show().

walkthrough.flow: new C().show() invokes C.show(), which calls A.super.show() and prints 'A'.
pitfalls: Omitting the public modifier when implementing or overriding an interface method in a class.

keyLines.note: A class can implement multiple interfaces.
Explicitly invokes interface A's default implementation.

importantPoints: An interface defines a contract that implementing classes agree to provide.
A class can implement multiple interfaces. Modern Java interfaces can contain abstract, default, static and private methods.
Java example to remember: interface.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Can an interface have fields?
followUpQuestions.answer: An interface cannot have mutable instance fields, because an interface is a type contract rather than an instantiated state container. Every field declared in an interface is implicitly `public static final` (a compile-time constant shared at the interface level).

walkthrough.approach: Declare a constant (`GST_RATE`) in an interface without explicit modifiers to show that it is implicitly `public static final`.

steps.title: Declare an interface constant
steps.detail: double GST_RATE = 0.18 inside TaxPolicy is automatically treated by javac as public static final double GST_RATE = 0.18.

steps.title: Reference the constant in an implementing class
steps.detail: Invoice implements TaxPolicy and uses GST_RATE inside applyTax(double).

steps.title: Compute the result
steps.detail: new Invoice().applyTax(100) adds 18% GST and prints 118.0.

walkthrough.flow: new Invoice().applyTax(100) reads the static constant TaxPolicy.GST_RATE (0.18), computes 100 + 18.0, and prints 118.0.
pitfalls: Trying to declare an uninitialized field or a private/protected field in an interface—interface fields must be initialized at declaration and are always public static final.

keyLines.note: Implicitly public static final; cannot be mutated or per-instance.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: State the three implicit modifiers on every interface field: `public`, `static`, and `final`—and mention that putting mutable objects (like an array) in an interface constant is an anti-pattern.

followUpQuestions.question: Can an interface extend multiple interfaces?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes. While a Java class can `extends` only one superclass, an interface can `extends` multiple parent interfaces (`interface SmartDevice extends Connectable, Rechargeable`), combining all of their abstract and default method contracts into one sub-interface.

walkthrough.approach: Combine two single-responsibility interfaces (`Readable` and `Writable`) into a composite sub-interface (`ReadWriteChannel`) using `extends`.

steps.title: Define granular parent interfaces
steps.detail: Readable declares read() and Writable declares write(String).

steps.title: Extend multiple interfaces
steps.detail: interface ReadWriteChannel extends Readable, Writable inherits both abstract method requirements.

steps.title: Implement the combined sub-interface
steps.detail: MemoryBuffer implements ReadWriteChannel and must provide both read() and write(String).

walkthrough.flow: Main creates MemoryBuffer as a ReadWriteChannel, calls channel.write('OK') to store the string, and calls channel.read() to print 'OK'.
pitfalls: Writing interface ReadWriteChannel implements Readable, Writable—interfaces use extends, never implements, when inheriting from other interfaces!

keyLines.note: An interface uses extends (not implements) to inherit from multiple interfaces.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Watch out for the syntax trap interviewers love: a class `implements` interfaces, but an interface `extends` other interfaces (and can extend more than one).

conceptual.question: Interface versus abstract class: when would you use each?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Use an interface for a capability or contract; use an abstract class when related classes should share state or common implementation.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: A class can implement multiple interfaces but extend only one class. Decide based on the relationship and expected evolution.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: Flyable can be implemented by Bird and Drone; AbstractVehicle can share common vehicle state.

walkthrough.approach: Use an abstract base class (`Shape`) when related subtypes share construction or state, and require subclasses (`Circle`) to implement `area()`.

steps.title: Share base initialization in Shape
steps.detail: Shape() runs common initialization for all shapes.

steps.title: Defer subtype-specific math via abstract area()
steps.detail: Circle implements area() using its private radius r.

walkthrough.flow: new Circle(2) runs Shape() ('Shape initialized') and then Circle(2); calling area() > 0 prints 'true'.
pitfalls: Using an abstract class for a capability shared by unrelated classes—use an interface instead so subclasses don't waste their single extends slot.

keyLines.note: Use an abstract class when subclasses are closely related and share state/constructors.

importantPoints: Use an interface for a capability or contract; use an abstract class when related classes should share state or common implementation.
A class can implement multiple interfaces but extend only one class. Decide based on the relationship and expected evolution.
Java example to remember: abstract.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Can an abstract class implement an interface?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes. An abstract class can implement an interface and provide shared implementations for some methods while leaving the remaining interface methods unimplemented for concrete subclasses to complete.

walkthrough.approach: Use an abstract base class (`BaseExporter`) to implement shared interface boilerplate (`validate()`) while deferring format-specific work (`exportData()`) to concrete subclasses.

steps.title: Define the full interface contract
steps.detail: Exporter requires both validate() and exportData().

steps.title: Implement shared behavior in an abstract class
steps.detail: BaseExporter implements Exporter and defines validate(), leaving exportData() unimplemented because BaseExporter is abstract.

steps.title: Complete the contract in a concrete subclass
steps.detail: CsvExporter extends BaseExporter and implements the remaining exportData() method.

walkthrough.flow: Main creates CsvExporter referenced as Exporter. Calling exporter.validate() runs the inherited BaseExporter.validate() ('Common validation'), and exporter.exportData() runs CsvExporter.exportData() ('Exporting CSV').
pitfalls: Forgetting that the concrete subclass at the bottom of the hierarchy must implement every interface method not already implemented by its abstract superclasses.

keyLines.note: Skeletal implementation pattern: implements part of Exporter and leaves the rest abstract.
Concrete class needs to implement only the remaining exportData() method.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Name this pattern! In the JDK, pairing an interface with an abstract base class (`List` + `AbstractList`, `Map` + `AbstractMap`) is called the *Skeletal Implementation* pattern (Effective Java Item 20).

followUpQuestions.question: Can an interface have default methods?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes. Since Java 8, interfaces can declare `default` methods with a body so new operations can be added to existing interfaces without breaking implementing classes. However, unlike abstract classes, default methods cannot access mutable instance fields or `protected` state.

walkthrough.approach: Define a `default` convenience method (`sendUrgent`) on an interface that delegates to the abstract contract method (`send`).

steps.title: Declare the core abstract method
steps.detail: Notifier declares void send(String msg) as the single method implementers must write.

steps.title: Build a default method on top of the abstract method
steps.detail: default void sendUrgent(String msg) prepends '[URGENT] ' and calls this.send(...).

steps.title: Inherit the default behavior automatically
steps.detail: EmailNotifier implements only send(String) and gets sendUrgent(String) for free.

walkthrough.flow: Main calls n.sendUrgent('Server down'), which executes Notifier.sendUrgent. Inside sendUrgent, the call to send('[URGENT] Server down') dynamically dispatches to EmailNotifier.send(), printing 'Email: [URGENT] Server down'.
pitfalls: Thinking default methods make abstract classes obsolete—abstract classes are still required whenever shared methods need constructors, non-static fields, or non-public (protected/package-private) members.

keyLines.note: Default method implemented purely in terms of the interface's abstract send() method.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Contrast default methods with abstract classes: 'Default methods are great for stateless convenience methods that delegate to abstract interface methods, but only abstract classes can hold instance state.'

conceptual.question: What is the difference between IS-A and HAS-A?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: IS-A describes inheritance and substitutability; HAS-A describes one object containing or using another.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: Use inheritance when a subtype can safely stand in for its parent. Use composition when one class collaborates with another.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: Car IS-A Vehicle; Car HAS-A Engine.

walkthrough.approach: Model an `IS-A` relationship (`Employee extends Person`) where every `Employee` is substitutable for a `Person`.

steps.title: Define parent type Person
steps.detail: Person holds shared identity state (name).

steps.title: Specialize with extends
steps.detail: Employee extends Person establishes that an Employee IS-A Person and initializes name via super(name).

walkthrough.flow: new Employee('Mira') initializes Person.name = 'Mira' via super('Mira'), and introduce() prints 'Mira'.
pitfalls: Using extends for HAS-A relationships (like Car extending Engine).

keyLines.note: Models IS-A inheritance; use a field reference for HAS-A composition.

importantPoints: IS-A describes inheritance and substitutability; HAS-A describes one object containing or using another.
Use inheritance when a subtype can safely stand in for its parent. Use composition when one class collaborates with another.
Java example to remember: inheritance.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Why is HAS-A often more flexible?
followUpQuestions.answer: `HAS-A` (composition) is more flexible than `IS-A` (inheritance) because a composed field can hold an interface reference that is injected or swapped at runtime, whereas `extends` permanently binds a subclass to one concrete parent class at compile time.

walkthrough.approach: Use `HAS-A` composition (`Cart` holds a `DiscountPolicy` reference) to swap discount algorithms on the same `Cart` instance at runtime.

steps.title: Extract varying behavior into an interface
steps.detail: DiscountPolicy defines apply(int price) with FestivalDiscount and VipDiscount implementations.

steps.title: Compose the policy inside Cart
steps.detail: Cart holds a DiscountPolicy field instead of extending a discount class.

steps.title: Swap the collaborator at runtime
steps.detail: Main computes checkout(1000) with FestivalDiscount (900), swaps to VipDiscount via setPolicy(), and computes 750 on the same Cart.

walkthrough.flow: cart starts with FestivalDiscount and prints 900. Calling cart.setPolicy(new VipDiscount()) replaces the composed collaborator at runtime, so the second cart.checkout(1000) prints 750.
pitfalls: Modeling discounts with inheritance (FestivalCart extends Cart, VipCart extends Cart), which makes it impossible to change a cart's discount type without creating a brand-new Cart object.

keyLines.note: HAS-A field typed to the interface allows runtime swapping.
Changes behavior on the live object—impossible with compile-time inheritance.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Point out that swapping a `HAS-A` interface collaborator at runtime is the exact basis of the Gang of Four *Strategy* pattern.

followUpQuestions.question: Can a class have both relationships?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes. Real-world classes routinely combine both: a class can extend a base class or implement an interface (`IS-A`) while simultaneously holding collaborator objects as fields (`HAS-A`). For example, `ElectricCar extends Vehicle` (`IS-A`) and contains a `private final Battery battery` (`HAS-A`).

walkthrough.approach: Model `ElectricCar` with both an `IS-A` superclass (`extends Vehicle`) and a `HAS-A` component (`private final Battery battery`).

steps.title: Establish the IS-A hierarchy
steps.detail: ElectricCar extends Vehicle because an electric car is a genuine subtype of Vehicle.

steps.title: Embed the HAS-A component
steps.detail: ElectricCar holds a private final Battery field because a car has a battery rather than being a battery.

steps.title: Combine inherited and composed behavior
steps.detail: status() calls the inherited move() method and reads the composed battery.charge field.

walkthrough.flow: new ElectricCar().status() invokes inherited Vehicle.move() ('Vehicle moving') and then reads its composed Battery instance ('Battery: 95%').
pitfalls: Treating IS-A and HAS-A as mutually exclusive—use IS-A for the core taxonomic identity and HAS-A for internal components and services.

keyLines.note: IS-A relationship: ElectricCar is a subtype of Vehicle.
HAS-A relationship: ElectricCar owns a Battery component.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Use `ElectricCar extends Vehicle` (IS-A) with a `Battery` field (HAS-A) as a crisp, intuitive example showing how both relationships coexist.

conceptual.question: What is composition in OOP?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Composition is a strong whole-part relationship in which the whole owns or controls the lifecycle of its parts.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: It is commonly implemented by keeping another object as a field and managing it as part of the owner.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: An Order may own OrderItems whose lifecycle is tied to the order.

walkthrough.approach: Model composition by having `Car` create and own a `private final Engine` field and delegate `start()` to it.

steps.title: Define the component class
steps.detail: Engine provides void start().

steps.title: Compose Engine inside Car
steps.detail: Car declares private final Engine engine = new Engine(), tying the engine's lifecycle to the car.

steps.title: Delegate behavior
steps.detail: Car.start() calls engine.start().

walkthrough.flow: new Car() constructs its internal Engine instance, and calling .start() delegates to engine.start(), printing 'Engine started'.
pitfalls: Exposing the private Engine field via a public setter or mutable reference when Car is supposed to own it exclusively.

keyLines.note: Car owns the lifecycle of its Engine component.
Delegates engine startup to the composed component.

importantPoints: Composition is a strong whole-part relationship in which the whole owns or controls the lifecycle of its parts.
It is commonly implemented by keeping another object as a field and managing it as part of the owner.
Java example to remember: composition.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Composition versus aggregation?
followUpQuestions.answer: Both are whole-part (`HAS-A`) relationships, but they differ in lifecycle ownership. In **composition**, the whole creates and exclusively owns the part (if an `Order` is deleted, its `OrderItem`s cease to exist). In **aggregation**, the whole references parts that have an independent lifecycle (if a `Department` closes, its `Professor`s still exist).

walkthrough.approach: Contrast aggregation (injecting an externally created `Professor` into `Department`) with composition (`Order` privately constructing and owning its `OrderItem`).

steps.title: Model aggregation with external lifecycle
steps.detail: Main creates Professor('Dr. Rao') outside Department and passes the reference in; prof survives even if dept is discarded.

steps.title: Model composition with exclusive internal ownership
steps.detail: Order constructs new OrderItem(sku) inside its own constructor and keeps OrderItem private so nothing outside Order can reference it.

walkthrough.flow: Main creates Professor('Dr. Rao') and passes it to Department, while Order('BOOK-1') internally constructs its private OrderItem. Printing both outputs 'Dr. Rao | BOOK-1'.
pitfalls: Exposing a getter that returns a direct reference to a composed part, which lets external callers hold onto the part and blurs composition into aggregation.

keyLines.note: Aggregation: Department receives an existing Professor with an independent lifecycle.
Composition: Order creates and exclusively owns its OrderItem.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: In database/JPA terms, compare composition to `CascadeType.ALL` + `orphanRemoval = true` (`Order` -> `OrderItem`) and aggregation to a nullable foreign key (`Department` -> `Professor`).

followUpQuestions.question: How does composition differ from inheritance?
followUpQuestions.answer: Inheritance (`extends`) is white-box reuse: the subclass inherits the parent's public/protected API and is coupled to parent implementation details at compile time. Composition is black-box reuse: the owner holds a `private` reference to a collaborator and delegates specific calls, keeping its public API clean and decoupled.

walkthrough.approach: Wrap an `Engine` inside `Car` as a `private final` field and explicitly forward `start()` rather than inheriting `Engine`'s class hierarchy.

steps.title: Encapsulate the collaborator
steps.detail: Car declares private final Engine engine = new Engine() so callers of Car cannot access Engine directly.

steps.title: Expose only intentional methods
steps.detail: Car defines void start() and delegates to engine.start(), hiding any other internal Engine helper methods.

walkthrough.flow: new Car().start() invokes Car.start(), which forwards the call to its private engine.start() method and prints 'Engine started'.
pitfalls: Using inheritance when you only want one method from a class, which unintentionally exposes all of the parent class's public methods to your callers.

keyLines.note: Black-box reuse: Engine is hidden inside Car.
Explicit delegation forwards only the operation Car wants to expose.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Use the terms *white-box reuse* (inheritance—internals visible to subclasses) vs. *black-box reuse* (composition—interacts only through the collaborator's public contract).

conceptual.question: What is association?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Association is a general relationship in which objects know about or collaborate with one another.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: It may be one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many, and unidirectional or bidirectional. It is a design relationship, not a Java keyword.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: A Doctor treats Patients; either side may hold a reference depending on the model.

walkthrough.approach: Model a general `USES-A` association where a `Doctor` collaborates with an independent `Patient` object via `treat(Patient)`.

steps.title: Define independent domain entities
steps.detail: Doctor and Patient each have their own independent lifecycle.

steps.title: Associate via a method interaction
steps.detail: Doctor.treat(Patient patient) uses the Patient reference without owning it.

walkthrough.flow: Main creates Doctor('Mehta') and Patient('Asha') independently and calls doc.treat(pat), printing 'Dr. Mehta treats Asha'.
pitfalls: Confusing association (peer collaboration, no ownership) with composition (exclusive whole-part lifecycle ownership).

keyLines.note: Doctor interacts with Patient via a reference without owning Patient's lifecycle.

importantPoints: Association is a general relationship in which objects know about or collaborate with one another.
It may be one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many, and unidirectional or bidirectional. It is a design relationship, not a Java keyword.
Java example to remember: polymorphism.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: What is multiplicity?
followUpQuestions.answer: Multiplicity (or cardinality) specifies how many instances of one class can be associated with one instance of another class—such as one-to-one (`1:1`, a `User` has one `Profile`), one-to-many (`1:N`, a `Course` has a `List<Student>`), or many-to-many (`M:N`, `Student`s and `Course`s).

walkthrough.approach: Express a one-to-many (`1:N`) multiplicity in Java by holding a `List<Student>` inside `Course`.

steps.title: Model the 'many' side
steps.detail: Student represents a single learner entity.

steps.title: Use a collection field for 1:N multiplicity
steps.detail: Course holds final List<Student> enrolled, allowing one Course instance to reference zero, one, or many Student instances.

steps.title: Populate and query the association
steps.detail: Main associates two Student objects with one Course and prints the enrolled count (2).

walkthrough.flow: Main creates two Student instances and passes them to new Course('Java OOP', ...). List.copyOf stores an unmodifiable list of size 2, and println outputs 'Java OOP: 2'.
pitfalls: Using a single reference field when domain requirements allow multiple associated items, or forgetting defensive copying (List.copyOf) on the collection.

keyLines.note: Collection type expresses a 1-to-many (1:N) multiplicity in Java code.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Explain how multiplicity maps to Java types: `1:1` is a single reference field (`Profile profile`), while `1:N` and `M:N` use collection fields (`List<Student>` or `Set<Student>`).

followUpQuestions.question: Is association a Java keyword?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. Unlike `extends` or `implements`, Java has no `associates`, `aggregates`, or `composes` keyword. Association is a domain-modeling concept expressed in Java through ordinary reference fields, collections, and method parameters.

walkthrough.approach: Show how a `USES-A` association between `ReportService` and `Printer` is written in plain Java using a method parameter without any special keyword.

steps.title: Define the collaborating type
steps.detail: Printer provides print(String doc).

steps.title: Express association via a method parameter or field
steps.detail: ReportService.export(Printer printer) accepts a Printer reference to collaborate with it.

steps.title: Execute the collaboration
steps.detail: Main passes new Printer() into export(), printing 'Printing: Q4 Summary'.

walkthrough.flow: Main instantiates ReportService and Printer, passing the Printer reference to export(printer). export() invokes printer.print('Q4 Summary').
pitfalls: Thinking UML arrows (association, aggregation, composition) have distinct compiler keywords in Java—the compiler only sees reference variables and method parameters.

keyLines.note: Expresses a USES-A association through a standard object reference parameter.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: State clearly: 'Inheritance has keywords (`extends`, `implements`), whereas association, aggregation, and composition are expressed through object references and lifecycle rules.'

conceptual.question: What are access modifiers in Java?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Access modifiers control where classes and members can be accessed.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: Java provides public, protected, package-private (no modifier), and private. They help enforce encapsulation and API boundaries.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: A private balance field is accessible only inside its declaring class.

walkthrough.approach: Demonstrate `private`, `protected`, and `public` visibility on `Vault` and access the `private` field through a `public` method.

steps.title: Hide internal state with private
steps.detail: private String secret is accessible only inside Vault.

steps.title: Expose subclass/package and public members
steps.detail: protected String hint and public String label are visible to Main in the same package.

steps.title: Provide controlled access via revealSecret()
steps.detail: public String revealSecret() safely returns secret.

walkthrough.flow: Main reads v.label, v.hint, and v.revealSecret() on Vault, printing 'public-vault | subclass-visible | top-secret'.
pitfalls: Making fields public or protected by default instead of starting with private and widening only when required.

keyLines.note: Accessible only within the Vault class body.
Public accessor exposes the secret in a controlled way.

importantPoints: Access modifiers control where classes and members can be accessed.
Java provides public, protected, package-private (no modifier), and private. They help enforce encapsulation and API boundaries.
Java example to remember: polymorphism.
Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: What does protected mean across packages?
followUpQuestions.answer: Across packages, a `protected` member can be accessed by a subclass **only through `this`, `super`, or a reference typed as that subclass (or a further subclass)**. A subclass in another package cannot access a `protected` member on a plain `Parent` reference (`new Parent().protectedField` fails compilation across packages).

walkthrough.approach: Access a `protected` superclass field (`prefix`) from a subclass (`AppLogger`) through `this.prefix`.

steps.title: Declare a protected member in the superclass
steps.detail: BaseLogger marks prefix as protected so subclasses (even in different packages) can inherit it.

steps.title: Access via the subclass receiver (this)
steps.detail: AppLogger.log() reads this.prefix, which is legal both within the same package and across packages.

walkthrough.flow: new AppLogger().log('Started') reads the inherited protected field this.prefix ('[LOG]') and prints '[LOG] Started'.
pitfalls: Assuming a subclass in package B can write BaseLogger b = new BaseLogger(); System.out.println(b.prefix); when BaseLogger is in package A—cross-package protected access requires the receiver expression to be of type AppLogger (or a subtype), not BaseLogger!

keyLines.note: Accessible to all classes in the same package and to subclasses in other packages via subclass references.
Accessing via this (an AppLogger reference) satisfies Java's cross-package protected rule.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Mention the subtle JLS rule (§6.6.2): in a different package, a subclass can access `protected` members on `this` or a `Child` reference, but *not* on a standalone `new Parent()` instance!

followUpQuestions.question: Can a top-level class be private?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. A top-level class or interface can only be declared `public` or package-private (no access modifier). Declaring a top-level class `private` or `protected` is a compile-time error because nothing outside the file/package hierarchy could meaningfully scope it; however, **nested/inner classes** inside an outer class *can* be `private` or `protected`.

walkthrough.approach: Show that while `Main` (a top-level class) uses `public`, a nested helper class (`SecretHelper`) inside `Main` can legally be declared `private`.

steps.title: Top-level class uses public or package-private
steps.detail: public class Main is a top-level declaration; javac only permits public or default package-private here.

steps.title: Nested class uses private
steps.detail: private static class SecretHelper is a member of Main, so it can use any of the four access modifiers, including private.

steps.title: Instantiate the private nested class inside its enclosing class
steps.detail: Main.main creates new SecretHelper() and prints its message.

walkthrough.flow: Main.main instantiates its private static nested class SecretHelper and calls message(), printing 'Private nested class allowed'.
pitfalls: Saying 'no class can ever be private in Java'—always qualify that *top-level* classes cannot be private/protected, whereas *nested* classes can use all four modifiers.

keyLines.note: Top-level class: only public or package-private is legal.
Nested member class: private and protected are both legal here.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Always distinguish *top-level classes* (only `public` or package-private) from *nested/inner classes* (all four modifiers allowed, e.g., `private static class Node` inside `LinkedList`).

conceptual.question: Static versus instance members: what is the difference?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Static members belong to the class; instance members belong to each object.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: A static field is shared by instances. Instance methods can access instance and static state, while static methods have no this reference.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: Employee.companyName can be static while employee.name is an instance field.

walkthrough.approach: Contrast `static` class-level members with instance members by accessing `ref.type` and `ref.print()` through a `Parent` reference.

steps.title: Declare static members on Parent and Child
steps.detail: static String type and static void print() belong to their declaring class, not to individual instances.

steps.title: Access via a Parent-typed reference
steps.detail: Parent ref = new Child(); binds both ref.type and ref.print() to Parent at compile time.

walkthrough.flow: Because static members are bound at compile time using the declared reference type (Parent), both ref.type and ref.print() output 'Parent'.
pitfalls: Accessing static members via an instance variable (ref.print()) instead of the class name (Parent.print()).

keyLines.note: Class-level field shared across all instances of Parent.
Static method call resolves at compile time to Parent.print().

importantPoints: Static members belong to the class; instance members belong to each object.
A static field is shared by instances. Instance methods can access instance and static state, while static methods have no this reference.

Mention the limitation or compile-time/runtime rule when relevant.

followUpQuestions.question: Can a static method directly access an instance field?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. A `static` method has no `this` reference because it can be called on the class itself without any object existing. To access an instance field inside a `static` method, you must either create or receive an explicit object reference (e.g., `user.name`).

walkthrough.approach: Pass an explicit `User` instance into a `static` method so it can read the `name` instance field without an implicit `this` reference.

steps.title: Declare an instance field
steps.detail: String name = 'Asha' belongs to each individual User object on the heap.

steps.title: Pass an object reference to the static method
steps.detail: static void printUser(User u) has no implicit this, so it reads u.name through the explicit parameter u.

walkthrough.flow: Main creates new User() and passes it to User.printUser(u), which dereferences u.name and prints 'Asha'.
pitfalls: Writing System.out.println(name); directly inside a static method, which fails with 'non-static variable name cannot be referenced from a static context'.

keyLines.note: Static method has no implicit this reference.
Reads the instance field through an explicit User object reference.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Give the exact mental model: 'Every instance method has a hidden first parameter `this`; a `static` method does not have `this`, so it doesn't know which object's instance field you mean unless you pass an object in.'

followUpQuestions.question: Can static methods be overridden?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. `static` methods are resolved at compile time using the reference type or class name (`invokestatic`), so they do not participate in runtime polymorphism. Declaring a `static` method with the same signature in a subclass **hides** the superclass method rather than overriding it.

walkthrough.approach: Show that calling a `static` method through a `Parent` reference (`ref.print()`) executes `Parent.print()` even when `ref` points to a `Child` instance.

steps.title: Define matching static methods in Parent and Child
steps.detail: Child.print() hides Parent.print() rather than overriding it.

steps.title: Invoke through a Parent-typed reference
steps.detail: Parent ref = new Child(); ref.print() is bound by javac at compile time to Parent.print().

walkthrough.flow: javac inspects the compile-time type of ref (Parent) and binds both ref.type and ref.print() to Parent, printing 'Parent' twice.
pitfalls: Placing @Override on a static method in a subclass—javac immediately rejects it with 'method does not override or implement a method from a supertype'.

keyLines.note: Compile-time type is Parent; static members ignore the runtime Child object.
Compiled as Parent.print() using static binding.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Contrast *method overriding* (runtime binding on instance methods) with *method hiding* (compile-time binding on static methods).

conceptual.question: What is dynamic method dispatch?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Dynamic method dispatch is runtime selection of an overridden instance method based on the actual object.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: The reference type controls which members are accessible at compile time, while the runtime class selects the overridden implementation.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: Animal animal = new Dog(); animal.sound() executes Dog.sound().

walkthrough.approach: Upcast a `Dog` instance to an `Animal` reference and trace how `a.sound()` selects `Dog.sound()` at runtime.

steps.title: Define overridable method on Animal
steps.detail: Animal declares void sound().

steps.title: Override sound() in Dog
steps.detail: Dog overrides sound() to print 'bark'.

steps.title: Invoke via Animal reference
steps.detail: Animal a = new Dog(); a.sound() uses dynamic method dispatch to run Dog.sound().

walkthrough.flow: At compile time, javac verifies sound() exists on Animal. At runtime, the JVM checks the actual heap object (Dog) and executes Dog.sound() ('bark').
pitfalls: Assuming dynamic method dispatch applies to fields or static methods—it applies only to overridden instance methods.

keyLines.note: Reference type is Animal; runtime object is Dog.
JVM dispatches to Dog.sound() at runtime.

importantPoints: Dynamic method dispatch is runtime selection of an overridden instance method based on the actual object.
The reference type controls which members are accessible at compile time, while the runtime class selects the overridden implementation.

followUpQuestions.question: Does field access use dynamic dispatch?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. Instance fields in Java never use dynamic dispatch. If a subclass declares a field with the same name as a superclass field, the subclass field **hides** the superclass field, and field access (`ref.value`) is resolved strictly at compile time using the declared reference type.

walkthrough.approach: Access both a shadowed field (`p.value`) and an overridden method (`p.show()`) on the exact same `Parent p = new Child()` reference to contrast compile-time field lookup with runtime method dispatch.

steps.title: Hide the field and override the method in Child
steps.detail: Child declares String value = 'child' (field hiding) and @Override void show() (method overriding).

steps.title: Resolve p.value at compile time
steps.detail: Because p is declared as Parent, p.value reads the Parent.value slot ('parent').

steps.title: Resolve p.show() at runtime
steps.detail: Because show() is an overridden instance method, p.show() dispatches to the runtime object's Child.show() ('child method').

walkthrough.flow: On Parent p = new Child(), p.value uses compile-time field resolution to print 'parent', while p.show() uses runtime vtable dispatch to print 'child method'.
pitfalls: Declaring duplicate field names in a subclass expecting getters inherited from the parent class to read the subclass field—inherited parent methods still read the parent's own field!

keyLines.note: Field access uses the compile-time reference type (Parent) -> prints 'parent'.
Overridden instance method uses the runtime heap type (Child) -> prints 'child method'.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Keep this contrast ready: on `Parent p = new Child()`, `p.field` prints the Parent field (compile-time binding), while `p.method()` runs the Child method (runtime dispatch).

followUpQuestions.question: Do overloaded methods use runtime dispatch?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. Overloaded methods are selected at compile time (`static binding`) based on the declared compile-time types of the arguments, not their runtime object types. In Java, only the receiver (`this` before the dot) is dynamically dispatched at runtime (`single dispatch`).

walkthrough.approach: Pass an upcast `Animal pet = new Dog()` reference to an overloaded `Vet.check(...)` method to prove that Java picks the overload using the compile-time argument type (`Animal`).

steps.title: Declare overloads for Animal and Dog
steps.detail: Vet overloads check(Animal) and check(Dog).

steps.title: Upcast Dog to an Animal reference
steps.detail: Animal pet = new Dog() has compile-time type Animal and runtime type Dog.

steps.title: Bind overload at compile time
steps.detail: javac inspects the declared type of the argument pet (Animal) and binds new Vet().check(pet) to check(Animal).

walkthrough.flow: Even though pet points to a Dog at runtime, javac already bound check(pet) to Vet.check(Animal) at compile time, so it prints 'Checking Animal'.
pitfalls: Expecting new Vet().check(pet) to print 'Checking Dog'—Java is a single-dispatch language (runtime type of arguments never changes which overload is chosen).

keyLines.note: Declared compile-time type of pet is Animal.
Overload resolution uses pet's compile-time type (Animal), selecting check(Animal).

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Use this exact `check(Animal)` vs `check(Dog)` snippet in interviews—it's the clearest demonstration that Java has *single dispatch* (only the receiver object before the `.` is polymorphic, never the arguments).

conceptual.question: What is the Object class in Java?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: java.lang.Object is the root superclass of Java classes that do not explicitly extend another class.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: It provides methods such as toString(), equals(), hashCode() and getClass().
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: A custom Employee class inherits Object methods unless it overrides them.

codeExample.output:
Asha is working
Ravi is working

walkthrough.approach: Show that every Java class implicitly extends `java.lang.Object` and inherits base contracts (`toString`, `equals`, `hashCode`, `getClass`).

steps.title: Implicitly extend java.lang.Object
steps.detail: class Employee has no extends clause, so the compiler makes it extend java.lang.Object automatically.

steps.title: Instantiate and invoke behavior
steps.detail: Employee instances inherit Object's methods alongside their own work() method.

walkthrough.flow: Main creates two Employee instances ('Asha' and 'Ravi') that implicitly inherit from Object, and invokes work() on each.
pitfalls: Calling == or failing to override equals() and hashCode() on domain classes stored in HashSet or HashMap.

keyLines.note: Implicitly extends java.lang.Object.

importantPoints: java.lang.Object is the root superclass of Java classes that do not explicitly extend another class.
It provides methods such as toString(), equals(), hashCode() and getClass().

followUpQuestions.question: Why override toString()?
followUpQuestions.answer: The default `Object.toString()` returns `ClassName@HexHashCode` (such as `Employee@4eec7777`), which tells you nothing about the object's state in logs or debugger views. Overriding `toString()` provides a human-readable summary of key fields whenever the object is printed or concatenated with a `String`.

walkthrough.approach: Override `Object.toString()` on `Employee` so `System.out.println` prints domain fields instead of the default class-name-and-hashcode string.

steps.title: Store key state fields
steps.detail: Employee holds id and name initialized in its constructor.

steps.title: Override public String toString()
steps.detail: Formats id and name into 'Employee{id=7, name=\'Asha\'}'.

steps.title: Pass object directly to println
steps.detail: System.out.println(Object) automatically calls String.valueOf(obj), which invokes obj.toString().

walkthrough.flow: System.out.println(new Employee(7, 'Asha')) calls Employee.toString() and prints "Employee{id=7, name='Asha'}".
pitfalls: Including sensitive fields (like passwords, tokens, or PII) inside toString(), which leaks secrets into application logs whenever an object is logged.

keyLines.note: Overrides Object.toString() to return diagnostic state.
println automatically invokes the overridden toString() method.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Mention production security: always override `toString()` for debugging clarity, but exclude passwords, tokens, and lazy-loaded JPA collections from `toString()`.

followUpQuestions.question: What contract links equals() and hashCode()?
followUpQuestions.answer: The `equals()` and `hashCode()` contract states: (1) if `a.equals(b)` is `true`, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` **must** be `true`; (2) if `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()`, `a.equals(b)` does not have to be `true` (hash collision). Violating this breaks hash-based collections like `HashMap` and `HashSet`.

walkthrough.approach: Override both `equals(Object)` and `hashCode()` using the same `id` field so a `HashSet` recognizes two distinct `new User(7)` instances as the same logical element.

steps.title: Compare logical identity in equals(Object)
steps.detail: Uses Java 16+ pattern matching (o instanceof User u && id == u.id) to compare id values safely.

steps.title: Compute a consistent bucket hash in hashCode()
steps.detail: Integer.hashCode(id) ensures two equal User(7) instances land in the exact same hash bucket.

steps.title: Verify lookup in a HashSet
steps.detail: users.contains(new User(7)) hashes to the same bucket and then confirms equality via equals(), returning true.

walkthrough.flow: users.add(new User(7)) places the object in the bucket for hashCode 7. users.contains(new User(7)) computes hashCode 7, inspects that bucket, calls equals() (which returns true), and prints 'true'.
pitfalls: Overriding equals() without overriding hashCode()—two equal objects get different identity hash codes from Object.hashCode(), so HashSet/HashMap looks in the wrong bucket and returns false!

keyLines.note: Pattern-matching instanceof safely handles null and checks logical equality.
Uses the exact same field (id) as equals() so equal objects share a hash code.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Walk through what `HashMap.get(key)` actually does: Step 1 compares `hashCode()` to find the bucket; Step 2 uses `==` and `equals()` inside the bucket. That immediately explains why overriding only `equals()` fails.

conceptual.question: What is the difference between == and equals()?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: For primitives, == compares values; for references, == compares identity. equals() compares logical equality when implemented for that purpose.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: Object.equals() defaults to identity comparison. Classes such as String override it for value equality.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: Two distinct String objects containing java may be == false but equals() true.

walkthrough.approach: Override `equals(Object)` and `hashCode()` on `User` so two distinct `new User(7)` heap instances compare as logically equal.

steps.title: Allocate two distinct heap objects
steps.detail: new User(7) and new User(7) have different memory addresses, so == would return false.

steps.title: Override equals(Object) for value equality
steps.detail: Checks o instanceof User u && id == u.id so two User objects with id == 7 are logically equal.

steps.title: Override hashCode() consistently
steps.detail: Integer.hashCode(id) guarantees equal User objects produce the same hash code.

walkthrough.flow: new User(7).equals(new User(7)) invokes User.equals(), matches instanceof User and 7 == 7, and prints 'true'.
pitfalls: Using == to compare String or wrapper objects for value equality, or overriding equals() without overriding hashCode().

keyLines.note: Compares logical state (id) rather than reference identity (==).
Maintains the Object contract that equal objects have equal hash codes.

importantPoints: For primitives, == compares values; for references, == compares identity. equals() compares logical equality when implemented for that purpose.
Object.equals() defaults to identity comparison. Classes such as String override it for value equality.
