followUpQuestions.question: What should equals() and hashCode() satisfy?
followUpQuestions.answer: `equals()` must be reflexive (`x.equals(x)`), symmetric (`x.equals(y) == y.equals(x)`), transitive, consistent, and return `false` for `null` (`x.equals(null) == false`). `hashCode()` must return the same integer for objects that are equal according to `equals()`.

walkthrough.approach: Verify symmetry, null-safety (`!u1.equals(null)`), and hash-code consistency on two distinct `User(7)` objects.

steps.title: Guarantee null safety with instanceof
steps.detail: o instanceof User u evaluates to false when o is null, avoiding NullPointerException without an explicit null check.

steps.title: Preserve equivalence relations
steps.detail: Comparing the immutable int id satisfies reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, and consistency.

steps.title: Align hashCode() with equals()
steps.detail: u1.hashCode() == u2.hashCode() holds because both derive from id = 7.

walkthrough.flow: u1.equals(u2) returns true, u1.equals(null) returns false, and u1.hashCode() == u2.hashCode() is true, so the combined boolean expression prints 'true'.
pitfalls: Using mutable fields in equals() and hashCode()—if you mutate a field after inserting the object into a HashSet, its hash code changes while it sits in the old bucket, losing the element forever.

keyLines.note: Automatically returns false when o is null or a different type.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Warn against using mutable fields in `equals`/`hashCode`: mutating a key after putting it into a `HashMap` changes its hash code while it remains in its old bucket!

followUpQuestions.question: How does == work for primitives?
followUpQuestions.answer: For primitive types (`int`, `long`, `double`, `boolean`, `char`, etc.), `==` compares the raw bit/numeric values directly. For reference types (`Integer`, `String`, custom objects), `==` compares memory references (object identity), which can trap developers when autoboxed wrappers outside the `[-128, 127]` cache are compared with `==`.

walkthrough.approach: Contrast `==` on primitive `int` values (`500 == 500`) against `==` and `.equals()` on autoboxed `Integer` wrapper objects outside the `IntegerCache` range (`-128` to `127`).

steps.title: Compare primitives by value
steps.detail: int a = 500; int b = 500; compares raw 32-bit integers, so a == b is true.

steps.title: Observe reference comparison on boxed Integer
steps.detail: Integer boxedA = 500 and boxedB = 500 autobox into two distinct Integer objects on the heap (since 500 > 127), so boxedA == boxedB is false.

steps.title: Compare wrapper value equality with equals()
steps.detail: boxedA.equals(boxedB) compares the underlying int values and returns true.

walkthrough.flow: a == b evaluates to true (primitive value match); boxedA == boxedB evaluates to false (distinct heap objects outside IntegerCache); boxedA.equals(boxedB) evaluates to true.
pitfalls: Testing Integer x = 100; Integer y = 100; x == y (which returns true due to IntegerCache[-128..127]) and assuming == works for all Integer values—it fails as soon as values hit 128!

keyLines.note: 500 is outside IntegerCache (-128 to 127), so autoboxing allocates a new Integer object.
Shows primitive == (true) vs wrapper == (false) vs wrapper .equals() (true).

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Bring up the `IntegerCache` (`-128` to `127`) trap when asked about `==` on primitives vs wrappers—it's a classic follow-up in Java interviews.

conceptual.question: Why is composition often preferred over inheritance?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: Composition lets a class delegate work to collaborators instead of locking behaviour into a class hierarchy.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: It reduces tight coupling, allows collaborators to be replaced, and avoids fragile base-class dependencies. Inheritance remains useful for genuine substitutability.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: OrderService has a PaymentGateway rather than extending a provider-specific gateway.

walkthrough.approach: Compose `Engine` inside `Car` as a `private final` collaborator and delegate `start()` instead of making `Car` extend `Engine`.

steps.title: Keep Engine as an independent collaborator
steps.detail: Engine encapsulates its own start() logic.

steps.title: Hold Engine as a private field in Car
steps.detail: Car declares private final Engine engine = new Engine().

steps.title: Delegate only the needed operation
steps.detail: Car.start() calls engine.start() without inheriting unwanted Engine internals.

walkthrough.flow: new Car().start() delegates to its internal engine.start() method and prints 'Engine started'.
pitfalls: Extending a concrete class just for code reuse when the subclass is not a true subtype of the parent.

keyLines.note: Composition decouples Car from Engine's inheritance hierarchy.

importantPoints: Composition lets a class delegate work to collaborators instead of locking behaviour into a class hierarchy.
It reduces tight coupling, allows collaborators to be replaced, and avoids fragile base-class dependencies. Inheritance remains useful for genuine substitutability.

followUpQuestions.question: When is inheritance appropriate?
followUpQuestions.answer: Inheritance is appropriate when (1) there is a genuine, permanent `IS-A` relationship where every subclass instance is 100% substitutable for the superclass (Liskov Substitution Principle), and (2) the superclass was explicitly designed and documented for extension (such as an `abstract` template class).

walkthrough.approach: Use an abstract template base class (`HttpServletLike`) with a `final` workflow method (`service`) and a `protected abstract` hook (`doGet`) designed specifically for subclass extension.

steps.title: Lock the invariant workflow as final
steps.detail: final void service(String) ensures subclasses cannot break the routing step.

steps.title: Expose a well-defined extension hook
steps.detail: protected abstract void doGet() documents the exact method subclasses should override.

steps.title: Specialize safely in the subclass
steps.detail: HealthCheckEndpoint extends HttpServletLike and implements doGet() to print '200 OK'.

walkthrough.flow: new HealthCheckEndpoint().service('GET') runs the final service() method on HttpServletLike, matches 'GET', and dispatches doGet() to HealthCheckEndpoint, printing '200 OK'.
pitfalls: Extending a concrete third-party class that was not designed for inheritance—a minor change to how its methods call each other in a future release can silently break your subclass.

keyLines.note: final prevents subclasses from breaking the superclass's core algorithm.
Explicit extension hook designed for subclasses.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Quote *Effective Java* Item 19: 'Design and document for inheritance or else prohibit it (make the class `final`).'

followUpQuestions.question: How does dependency injection support composition?
followUpQuestions.answer: Dependency injection (DI) separates **object creation** from **object use**. Instead of a composed class calling `new ConcreteCollaborator()` internally—which hard-wires the dependency—DI passes the collaborator in through the constructor (typed to an interface), making composition flexible and unit-testable.

walkthrough.approach: Combine composition (`OrderNotifier` holds a `MessageSender` field) with constructor injection so `OrderNotifier` never instantiates `SmsSender` itself.

steps.title: Compose via an interface field
steps.detail: OrderNotifier declares private final MessageSender sender.

steps.title: Inject the collaborator through the constructor
steps.detail: OrderNotifier(MessageSender sender) receives the implementation from outside (Main or a Spring IoC container).

steps.title: Delegate without knowing the concrete class
steps.detail: notifyPlaced() calls sender.send('Order placed'), printing 'SMS: Order placed'.

walkthrough.flow: Main constructs SmsSender and injects it into new OrderNotifier(...). Calling notifier.notifyPlaced() invokes sender.send('Order placed') on SmsSender.
pitfalls: Writing private final MessageSender sender = new SmsSender(); inside OrderNotifier—that is composition *without* dependency injection, which still tightly couples OrderNotifier to SmsSender.

keyLines.note: Composition: OrderNotifier HAS-A MessageSender.
Dependency injection: the caller supplies the concrete implementation.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Distinguish the two clearly: 'Composition means `OrderNotifier` holds a `MessageSender` field; Dependency Injection means `OrderNotifier` receives that `MessageSender` from outside instead of calling `new SmsSender()` itself.'

tricky.question: Can a constructor be inherited or overridden?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: No. Constructors are not inherited and cannot be overridden.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: A subclass constructor can invoke a superclass constructor using super(). Constructors can be overloaded within their own class.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: A Child constructor calls super() to initialize Parent state.

walkthrough.approach: Show that `Child` cannot inherit or override `Parent(String)`, and must instead invoke it explicitly via `super("...")`.

steps.title: Define parameterized parent constructor
steps.detail: Parent(String name) requires a String argument and prints it.

steps.title: Invoke parent constructor via super(...)
steps.detail: Child() calls super('parent initialized first') as its first statement.

walkthrough.flow: new Child() enters Child(), invokes super('parent initialized first') -> Parent(String) prints 'parent initialized first'.
pitfalls: Thinking a subclass inherits its parent's parameterized constructors automatically.

keyLines.note: Explicitly invokes the superclass constructor since constructors are not inherited.

importantPoints: No. Constructors are not inherited and cannot be overridden.
A subclass constructor can invoke a superclass constructor using super(). Constructors can be overloaded within their own class.

followUpQuestions.question: How is a superclass constructor selected?
followUpQuestions.answer: Every subclass constructor must invoke a superclass constructor first. If you do not write an explicit `super(...)` or `this(...)` call as the first statement, the compiler automatically inserts a no-argument `super();` call. If the superclass only has parameterized constructors and no accessible no-arg constructor, omitting `super(args)` causes a compile-time error.

walkthrough.approach: Trace the execution order when `new Child()` chains to `Base()` via `super()` before running its own constructor body.

steps.title: Enter Child() constructor
steps.detail: new Child() allocates memory for the combined Base+Child instance and invokes Child().

steps.title: Execute super() first
steps.detail: Before any statement in Child() can run, super() invokes Base(), which prints 'base'.

steps.title: Resume Child() body
steps.detail: Once Base() finishes, control returns to Child(), which prints 'child'.

walkthrough.flow: new Child() calls Child(), which immediately calls super() -> Base() prints 'base' -> Child() resumes and prints 'child'.
pitfalls: Declaring Base(String name) in the parent without Base(), and forgetting to write super('...') in Child()—javac inserts an implicit super() that fails to compile.

keyLines.note: Must be the first statement in Child(); inserted implicitly by javac if omitted.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: State the compiler rule: if a constructor doesn't start with `this(...)` or `super(...)`, `javac` inserts `super();`—which fails if the parent has only parameterized constructors.

tricky.question: If a parent reference points to a child object, which method and field are used?

interviewAnswer.shortAnswer: An overridden instance method uses the runtime object; a field is resolved using the reference's declared type.
interviewAnswer.detailedAnswer: Fields are hidden rather than overridden. The compile-time type determines field access, while dynamic dispatch selects overridden instance methods.
interviewAnswer.realWorldExample: Parent p = new Child(); p.value refers to Parent.value if accessible, but p.show() can call Child.show().

walkthrough.approach: Compare field access (`p.value`) and overridden method invocation (`p.show()`) on `Parent p = new Child()`.

steps.title: Hide the field and override the method
steps.detail: Child declares String value = 'child' (hiding Parent.value) and overrides void show().

steps.title: Resolve p.value using compile-time type
steps.detail: Because p is declared as Parent, p.value reads Parent.value ('parent').

steps.title: Resolve p.show() using runtime object type
steps.detail: Because p points to a Child instance, p.show() dispatches to Child.show() ('child method').

walkthrough.flow: p.value binds at compile time to Parent.value ('parent'); p.show() dispatches at runtime to Child.show() ('child method').

keyLines.note: Field access uses compile-time type Parent -> 'parent'.
Method override uses runtime object Child -> 'child method'.

importantPoints: An overridden instance method uses the runtime object; a field is resolved using the reference's declared type.
Fields are hidden rather than overridden. The compile-time type determines field access, while dynamic dispatch selects overridden instance methods.

followUpQuestions.answer: Java restricts multiple class inheritance to prevent the **diamond problem of state and constructors**: if class `D` extended both `B` and `C` (which both extended `A` with mutable fields and constructors), the JVM would face ambiguity over whether `D` holds one or two copies of `A`'s fields and which constructor (`B` or `C`) initializes `A`.

followUpQuestions.answer: The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) states that **no client or implementing class should be forced to depend on methods it does not use**. followUpQuestions.answer: Constructor injection is the practice of passing a class's required dependencies (`collaborators`) as parameters to its constructor and storing them in `private final` fields. It guarantees the object is never created in an incomplete state, makes dependencies explicit in the constructor signature, and allows unit tests to pass fake or mock implementations without a DI container.

followUpQuestions.question: What is the default value of an uninitialized instance int field?
followUpQuestions.answer: An uninitialized instance `int` field receives the default value **`0`** when the object is allocated on the heap (before any constructor runs). Similarly, `long` is `0L`, `double` is `0.0`, `boolean` is `false`, `char` is `'\u0000'`, and all object reference fields default to `null`. Local variables inside methods get **no** default value and must be explicitly assigned before reading.

steps.title: Base() runs before subclass field initializers

steps.title: Subclass field initializer assigns 8080
steps.detail: After Base() returns, ServerConfig's field initializer sets port = 8080, so reading cfg.port prints 'Port after ServerConfig(): 8080'.

pitfalls: Thinking int port = 8080; runs before super()—in Java bytecode, subclass instance field initializers are copied into the subclass constructor *after* the super() call!

keyLines.note: Starts at default 0 during Base(); assigned 8080 only after super() returns.

followUpQuestions.question: What is the difference between shallow and deep copying?
followUpQuestions.answer: A **shallow copy** copies only the outer container (or top-level object fields), so both the original and the copy still hold references to the exact same inner mutable elements. A **deep copy** duplicates both the container and every mutable element inside it so mutating an element in the copy cannot affect the original.

walkthrough.flow: new UserAccount('shreyas') delegates to UserAccount('shreyas', 'USER'), validates both arguments are non-null, assigns the final fields, and print() outputs 'shreyas:USER'.
pitfalls: Providing a no-arg constructor with setters for mandatory fields—callers can forget to call a setter and pass around a half-initialized object.

keyLines.note: Chains to the primary constructor with a sensible default for the optional role.
Fails fast at construction time if a mandatory argument is null.

followUpQuestions.interviewTip: Explain how `final` fields help at compile time: marking mandatory fields `private final` makes the Java compiler verify that every constructor path definitely assigns them!

codingExamples.title: Encapsulation using a BankAccount
codingExamples.interviewQuestion: Write a Java class that demonstrates encapsulation using a bank account.

walkthrough.approach: Protect `BankAccount.balance` as a `private` field and enforce positive amounts and sufficient funds inside `BankAccount` constructor, `deposit()`, and `withdraw()`.

steps.title: Validate initial state in the constructor
steps.detail: BankAccount(double openingBalance) rejects negative starting balances with IllegalArgumentException.

steps.title: Enforce deposit and withdrawal rules
steps.detail: deposit() requires amount > 0, and withdraw() verifies 0 < amount <= balance before subtracting.

steps.title: Read state through a controlled accessor
steps.detail: getBalance() returns the current balance after valid transactions complete.

walkthrough.flow: new BankAccount(1000) sets balance = 1000.0. deposit(500) increases it to 1500.0. withdraw(200) verifies 200 <= 1500, subtracts 200, and returns true. getBalance() prints 1300.0.
pitfalls: Exposing balance as public or providing an unvalidated setBalance(double) method, which allows callers to bypass withdrawal checks.

keyLines.note: Encapsulates account state so all mutations must pass through class methods.
Guards against negative withdrawals and overdrafts.

codingExamples.title: Runtime polymorphism using an interface
codingExamples.output:
Paid 500 using UPI
Paid 800 using card
codingExamples.interviewQuestion: Demonstrate runtime polymorphism using a payment interface.

walkthrough.approach: Use a single `Payment` interface reference to invoke `pay(int)` across both `UpiPayment` and `CardPayment` at runtime.

steps.title: Define the Payment interface
steps.detail: Declares void pay(int amount) as the uniform contract for all payment modes.

steps.title: Implement concrete payment channels
steps.detail: UpiPayment and CardPayment implement Payment with channel-specific output.

steps.title: Rebind the interface reference at runtime
steps.detail: Main points payment to UpiPayment and then CardPayment, calling payment.pay(...) identically each time.

walkthrough.flow: payment.pay(500) dispatches to UpiPayment ('Paid 500 using UPI'). Reassigning payment = new CardPayment() and calling payment.pay(800) dispatches to CardPayment ('Paid 800 using card').
pitfalls: Typing the variable as UpiPayment payment = new UpiPayment(), which prevents reassigning it to CardPayment later.

keyLines.note: Interface reference enables runtime polymorphism across implementations.
Swaps the concrete implementation without changing the call site.

codingExamples.title: Method overloading
codingExamples.interviewQuestion: Write an example of method overloading in Java.

walkthrough.approach: Overload `add` in `Calculator` with different parameter counts and types so the compiler binds each call site at compile time.

steps.title: Declare distinct parameter signatures
steps.detail: Calculator defines add(int, int), add(double, double), and add(int, int, int).

steps.title: Invoke with matching argument lists
steps.detail: Main calls calculator.add with two ints, two doubles, and three ints.

steps.title: Resolve statically at compile time
steps.detail: javac inspects the compile-time argument types and binds each call to its matching signature.

walkthrough.flow: calculator.add(2, 3) binds to add(int, int) and prints 5; add(2.5, 3.5) binds to add(double, double) and prints 6.0; add(1, 2, 3) binds to add(int, int, int) and prints 6.
pitfalls: Trying to overload by changing only the return type (e.g., double add(int a, int b))—javac rejects duplicate parameter signatures.

keyLines.note: Two-int overload selected when both arguments are int.
Two-double overload selected when either argument is double.

codingExamples.title: Method overriding and dynamic dispatch
codingExamples.interviewQuestion: Demonstrate method overriding and dynamic method dispatch.

walkthrough.approach: Override `Animal.sound()` in `Dog` and invoke `sound()` through an upcast `Animal` reference to demonstrate dynamic method dispatch.

steps.title: Declare base method in Animal
steps.detail: Animal defines void sound() as the overridable contract.

steps.title: Override in Dog with @Override
steps.detail: Dog replaces sound() with its own implementation that prints 'Bark'.

steps.title: Call via superclass reference
steps.detail: Animal animal = new Dog(); animal.sound() uses the runtime object type (Dog) to execute Dog.sound().

walkthrough.flow: Main upcasts new Dog() to Animal animal. When animal.sound() executes, the JVM looks up the actual object's class (Dog) and prints 'Bark'.
pitfalls: Thinking Animal animal = new Dog() calls Animal.sound() because the variable type is Animal—reference type only checks compile-time accessibility.

keyLines.note: Ensures Dog.sound() matches Animal.sound() signature.
Compile-time type is Animal; runtime object on the heap is Dog.

codingExamples.title: Inheritance and super
codingExamples.interviewQuestion: Write a Java example showing inheritance, constructor chaining and super.

walkthrough.approach: Chain subclass construction to the superclass with `super(name)` and extend inherited behavior by calling `super.display()` inside an overridden method.

steps.title: Initialize base state in Employee
steps.detail: Employee(String name) stores the employee's name and provides a base display() method.

steps.title: Forward constructor arguments via super(name)
steps.detail: Manager(String name) calls super(name) as its first statement to initialize the inherited name field.

steps.title: Extend overridden method behavior
steps.detail: Manager.display() calls super.display() to print the employee name before printing 'Role: Manager'.

walkthrough.flow: new Manager('Asha') invokes Manager('Asha'), which chains to Employee('Asha') and sets name = 'Asha'. Calling manager.display() runs Manager.display(), which calls super.display() ('Employee: Asha') and then prints 'Role: Manager'.
pitfalls: Calling display() inside Manager.display() without super., which causes infinite recursion and a StackOverflowError.

keyLines.note: Passes name up to the Employee constructor as the first statement.
Reuses the superclass implementation before adding Manager-specific output.

codingExamples.title: Composition instead of inheritance
codingExamples.interviewQuestion: Demonstrate composition using Car and Engine.

walkthrough.approach: Model `Car` HAS-A `Engine` using composition and constructor injection so `Car` delegates engine startup without inheriting from `Engine`.

steps.title: Create the independent component
steps.detail: Engine defines start() as a standalone collaborator.

steps.title: Compose Engine inside Car
steps.detail: Car holds a private final Engine field initialized through its constructor.

steps.title: Delegate operation in startCar()
steps.detail: Car.startCar() calls engine.start() and then adds its own car-level step.

walkthrough.flow: Main creates new Engine() and injects it into new Car(...). Calling car.startCar() invokes engine.start() ('Engine started') and then prints 'Car is ready'.
pitfalls: Making Car extend Engine just to call start()—a Car is not an Engine, and inheritance would expose internal Engine methods on Car.

keyLines.note: Composition: Car holds an Engine collaborator as a private final field.
Delegates engine-specific work to the composed collaborator.

codingExamples.title: Abstract class
codingExamples.interviewQuestion: Write an example using an abstract class and an abstract method.

walkthrough.approach: Define a shared `printArea()` template workflow in an abstract `Shape` class while deferring the `area()` formula to concrete subclasses like `Circle`.

steps.title: Declare abstract and concrete members in Shape
steps.detail: Shape declares abstract double area() alongside concrete void printArea().

steps.title: Implement the formula in Circle
steps.detail: Circle stores radius and overrides area() to return Math.PI * radius * radius.

steps.title: Invoke the template method
steps.detail: Calling shape.printArea() runs Shape.printArea(), which dynamically dispatches area() to Circle.area().

walkthrough.flow: new Circle(2) sets radius = 2.0. shape.printArea() calls this.area(), which dispatches at runtime to Circle.area() and prints 12.566370614359172.
pitfalls: Attempting new Shape() directly—abstract classes cannot be instantiated without a concrete subclass.

keyLines.note: Forces every concrete Shape subclass to supply an area calculation.
Concrete method in Shape calls the abstract hook, which dispatches to Circle at runtime.

codingExamples.title: Interface with constructor injection
codingExamples.interviewQuestion: Demonstrate interface-based design and constructor injection.

walkthrough.approach: Decouple `AlertService` from concrete notification channels by injecting a `NotificationSender` interface into its constructor.

steps.title: Define the NotificationSender interface
steps.detail: Declares send(String message) as the contract for all delivery channels.

steps.title: Implement Email and SMS senders
steps.detail: EmailSender and SmsSender each implement NotificationSender independently.

steps.title: Inject the abstraction into AlertService
steps.detail: AlertService accepts any NotificationSender in its constructor and delegates alert() to sender.send().

walkthrough.flow: Main injects new SmsSender() into new AlertService(...). Calling service.alert('Server is down') forwards the message to SmsSender.send(), printing 'SMS: Server is down'.
pitfalls: Instantiating new SmsSender() directly inside AlertService, which makes unit testing impossible without sending real SMS messages.

keyLines.note: Depends on the interface contract rather than a concrete sender class.
Constructor injection allows any implementation or test mock to be passed in.

keyTakeaways: Encapsulation protects object state and preserves invariants.
Abstraction exposes a useful contract while hiding implementation details.
Inheritance should model a genuine is-a relationship and preserve substitutability.
Polymorphism allows callers to work with a common type while implementations vary.
Overloading is resolved at compile time; overridden instance methods use runtime dispatch.
Prefer composition when a class needs another object’s capability rather than being a subtype of it.
Use interfaces for capabilities and contracts; use abstract classes when related types share state or implementation.
Know Java-specific rules around constructors, static methods, private methods, final methods, fields and access modifiers.
